#5026. Is Pilates Effective For Weight Loss? Instructors Share How To Incorporate It Into Your Routine

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s nearly impossible to scroll through social media right now without seeing some celebrity or influencer rave about the perks of Pilates. But even with all the buzz surrounding this popular practice, details are a little fuzzy on whether Pilates is an effective workout for weight loss.

First off, know that the health and fitness benefits of having a Pilates practice are so much more than that. This form of exercise is known for improving your posture, breathing, flexibility, and core strength. As Claudette Sariya, CPT, a personal trainer and fitness educator based in New York City, notes, “any movement that you can enjoy regularly and consistently can help you lose weight.”

So, doing Pilates (or any workout for that matter) to stay active paired with a nutrition plan is likely to help you with weight loss. But it probably won't help expedite your weight loss in the same way that, say, lifting heavy weights would. (We'll get into why!)

The focus of Pilates is not weight loss, experts point out. "Pilates should be considered part of your self-care routine," says Jacquelyn Brennan, CSCS, pilates instructor and co-founder of Chicago-based Pilates and Coffee. "We all need to move our spines more, move our joints through every range of motion, and everyone needs to be breathing better."

All of those healthy practices together can aid weight loss, though. Here's everything to know about doing Pilates when you're trying to lose weight.

Meet the experts: Gabbi Berkow, RD, CPT, is a nutritionist and Pilates instructor. Jacquelyn Brennan, CSCS, is a Pilates instructor and co-founder of Chicago-based Pilates and Coffee. Claudette Sariya, CPT, is a personal trainer and fitness educator based in New York City. Sonja R. Price Herbert is a certified Pilates instructor and founder of Black Girl Pilates. Nofar Hagag is a Pilates instructor and creator of the Nofar Method.

One form of Pilates isn't superior to another to drop pounds, experts agree. "For weight loss, I don’t think one type of Pilates is necessarily best,” says Berkow. Yet, there are different flavors—and finding one that you enjoy and will keep coming back to can, in turn, help you commit to a fitness routine and lose weight.

When someone mentions Pilates, they're often referring to Romana’s Pilates, which features exercises that Joseph Pilates (the founder) developed, explains Gabbi Berkow, RD, CPT, a nutritionist and Pilates instructor. Some studios are dedicated to classical or Romana’s Pilates (which is what Berkow is trained in) but there are studios that feature different Pilates-based workouts, which means they use Pilates-inspired moves but don't follow the classical version to a T. Some Pilates classes take place on a mat (a.k.a. mat Pilates), while others occur on a reformer, which is basically a sliding, spring-loaded platform.

You also might hear the term "athletic Pilates," but that is usually a description of the pace, says Sonja R. Price Herbert, a certified Pilates instructor and founder of Black Girl Pilates. These classes are designed to be fast-paced and high-intensity, and may even have some high-intensity interval training (HIIT) exercises and elements in the mix, which would make them better for weight loss due to the way HIIT training can help you burn more calories during and after the workout.

But if you really want to maximize your Pilates practice for weight loss and strength, it’s a good idea to use both the reformer and Cadillac machines, says Nofar Hagag, a Pilates instructor and creator of the Nofar Method. “By incorporating cardio-focused movements—such as squats, planks, and Pilates burpees, your heart rate increases, boosting calorie burn and metabolism,” she says. “These high-energy moves are paired with strength-training exercises, like side leg lifts and abs teasers, to build lean muscle and improve body composition.” (Reminder: Loading your muscles with resistance is key for muscle growth—and more muscle mass helps you burn more calories at rest and, in turn, lose weight.)

What you also want when it comes to Pilates and weight loss: an instructor who knows what they’re doing, is committed to safe movements, and who will challenge you, says Berkow. “You want to make sure your Pilates class is a workout. It shouldn’t be just a series of slow, easy stretches. Pilates has to contribute to your total daily calorie burn for it to make a difference in weight loss,” she says.

If you’ve ever gone to a class, you know how insane the core work is (seriously, the famed Hundreds exercise is not for the faint of heart...or abs).

While you cannot spot-reduce fat, Pilates can help you learn how to properly engage your pelvic floor and deep core muscles, says Brennan. "Pilates will teach you how to engage your muscles correctly, which will lend to increased activation during core exercises and lead to [the appearance of a] 'tighter tummy,' " she says.

However, to see abs definition, you do have to lose the fat that sits on top of your muscles, which requires proper nutrition, says Berkow. Think: a diet rich in whole, fresh foods and a limit on overly-processed foods and snacks.

There is some research to suggest that you can lose weight doing Pilates—but it's tough to give an exact number of pounds considering so many individual factors play into weight loss, such as genetics, sleep and stress, lifestyle habits, and more.

A meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2021 found that pilates “dramatically” reduced body weight and body fat percentage in adults with overweight or obesity. And the longer the person practiced Pilates, the bigger the weight loss. Older research has had mixed results, though, with one small study concluding Pilates was indeed helpful for weight loss, while another found it had no impact on weight loss in post-menopausal women.

You want a mat that offers a little extra cushion than the standard yoga mat to protect your vertebrae when rolling onto your back.

ProBody Pilates Ring And Mini Exercise Ball

Pilates teachers love a good prop. You may want to have a few options—like this Pilates ring (a.k.a. magic circle) and ball set—handy for online classes.

Many studios require sticky socks for both safety and sanitary reasons, so stashing a pair in your gym bag is always a good idea. These Pointe Studio socks offer a non-slip bottom in tons of cute colors and patterns.

Looking for a mat that's a bit more aesthetic? The 8mm-sized Bala Play Mat is another cushy option (and it’s antimicrobial, to boot!).

If you want to invest in your Pilates practice, this home reformer is a cult favorite that often shows up in professional studios. During testing, we found this machine to have a sleek, low profile, sturdy frame, and impressive footbar adjustability.

Again, traditional Pilates isn’t a modality designed for weight loss. Generally, traditional classes do not pack enough of a cardio or strength training component, Herbert says: “It is not a steady-state [cardio modality] like running, jumping, or walking. There is also not enough weight [or resistance] to aid in a decrease in body fat.” Instead, Herbert says that “Pilates focuses on awareness of the body, efficiency of movement, and breath.”

Pilates will, however, deliver far more benefits than just a lower number on a scale that may indirectly help with weight loss. For instance, Pilates involves breath work, encouraging deeper belly breaths that are in direct contrast to the shallow breathing many of us do on the regular. “Shallow breathing leads to increased cortisol levels, which contributes to weight gain. One could say that through pilates and learning to breathe better, you’d have lower cortisol—and thus, stress—levels, something that can help you lose weight,” Brennan says.

Feeling better, both mentally and physically, will also encourage you to take care of your body, says Berkow—and Pilates can definitely be a key part of achieving an overall weight-loss goal.

#5023. House Oversight Chair calls for possible ban on government officials’ prediction market bets over insider trading concerns

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Friday, the committee released its findings of an investigation it launched in May on insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials.

The Republican chair of the House Oversight Committee is calling for new limits on government officials' use of prediction markets, including the possibility of an outright ban, amid growing concerns that public officials could use insider information to profit from bets on the platforms.

On Friday, the committee released findings from an investigation it launched in May into insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials, military personnel, and those with security clearances. The committee sifted through 1,700 pages of documents and also received five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market companies, said Chair James Comer, R-Ky.

Concerns in Washington have intensified over the past year, particularly after an active-duty U.S. Army soldier who used confidential information to place bets on Polymarket ahead of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro's capture. Thereafter, others in government have also been found using inside information to make money on bets on prediction markets, including the White House's former teleprompter operator. Political candidates have also faced allegations of insider trading on the platforms.

"Congress must consider additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people's trust in government," Comer said on Friday.

Those reforms should be legislation that restricts which bets federal employees, lawmakers and congressional staff can place on prediction markets — or an outright ban, the committee said.

"Whether it's an outright prohibition on trading on prediction markets or restrictions on some subset of contracts like government-related contracts, applying these restrictions to officials in all branches of government would strengthen ethical expectations that government personnel should not personally and financially benefit from access to non-public information associated with their work as government servants…" according to the memo.

Congress should also have a role in encouraging prediction market companies and federal agencies to share necessary information to enforce restrictions, the committee said.

Both major prediction market companies — Kalshi and Polymarket — have said they have taken steps to tighten controls to prevent government officials from using inside information. Lawmakers have also begun addressing the issue themselves. In April, the Senate voted to pass a resolution to ban members from trading on prediction markets.

#5022. Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Bitcoin custody has always involved some degree of risk, but wallet manufacturers like Trezor—which build physical devices designed to keep a user’s private keys secure offline—are preparing for a post-quantum world where new challenges arise.

That’s because SHRINCS, the community’s leading candidate for a post-quantum signature scheme, allows users to make transactions using stateful signatures that require rigid state tracking to prevent funds from being stolen, according to Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka.

Proposed late last year by Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick and cryptographer Mikhail Kudinov, SHRINCS centers on a composite hash-based approach: users can make transactions using either stateful signatures or stateless signatures.

Stateless signatures are quite large—potentially affecting fees, signature speed, and other efficiency metrics—but are safe to reuse, while smaller, more efficient stateful signatures come with serious security risks when reused beyond a particular signing budget.

The stateful component of SHRINCS is made up of a tree of one-time signatures, and if these keys are accidentally used more than once, enough cryptographic information is revealed for someone else to forge that user’s signature and effectively steal funds.

If Bitcoin successfully adopts SHRINCS, maintaining a meticulous count of the wallet’s state will become a critical responsibility for wallet developers—with lots of potential edge-case security risks.

“You’re giving them an option to mess up,” Sušánka said during a recent episode of MARA Foundation TV, in reference to state tracking. “It’s our job to make it in a secure way, right? It shouldn't be the user’s job.”

To mitigate this risk, Trezor is weighing options for how to support secure UX in a post-quantum world. For instance, Sušánka said the company is considering making the heavier, slower stateless signatures the default setting for all users, tucking the riskier stateful option behind an advanced settings wall.

While Sušánka recognizes that SHRINCS may be the conservative cryptographic choice because it relies on the same cryptographic assumptions as SHA-256, he is “kind of torn on the topic because maintaining the state is a burden.”

“For example, you can have two Trezors with the same recovery seed. How do you share the state between those two? You really don’t,” he added.

“That being said, as it is with everything, this is about trade-offs,” Sušánka continued. “The [stateful] signatures are 10 times smaller ... That makes a big difference. So, I just don't want to throw it off the table completely.”

Sušánka went on to share that while many are focused on Bitcoin’s migration path to post-quantum addresses and signatures, hardware wallet devices will also need to be physically updated for full quantum protection. Most signing devices use quantum-vulnerable cryptography for hardware-specific security functions, like firmware and device authentication.

If users want to ensure their devices are secure in a post-quantum world, they will need to use “quantum-ready” devices—that is, devices that use post-quantum cryptography for device and firmware authentication as well.

In anticipation of these needs, the company is already shipping products like Trezor Safe 7 that support post-quantum cryptography for wallet authentication processes. Of course, transactions made on these devices will only be quantum-secure once Bitcoin itself upgrades to post-quantum security.

That said, Sušánka warned developers not to wait too long to give users migration options, as he believes the migration of potentially millions of users will take time.

“People should be ready to make compromises,” Sušánka said. “If we’re all going to be very strict on what can and cannot be done, we’re not going to get anywhere.”

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

LED face masks are usually class II devices. They’re either FDA-listed or FDA-registered, meaning the brand notified the agency about the device. However, this listing doesn’t indicate the products are approved, cleared, or authorized by the agency.

They could also be FDA-cleared, meaning they are similar to other devices that are legally marketed for the same use. Our editors prioritized testing face masks that are either FDA-listed, -registered, or -cleared. And I referenced the FDA database to verify the status of our recommendations.

If you’re photosensitive or have connective tissue conditions, you should either skip LED light therapy or approach it with caution, advises Dr. Ansell. If neither issue is a problem for you, Dr. Engelman suggests wearing it a few times a week, but it's crucial to refer to your specific mask's instructions for the recommended time.

Start with clean skin, says Dr. Engelman. After washing your face in the morning or at night, set your mask to the proper wavelength, then put on goggles. Comfort is key, so feel free to adjust any straps and align yourself with the cushioning (if your mask has any) before using it. Post-use, finish the rest of your skincare routine, and definitely use it before applying retinol, says Dr. Shirazi.

#5016. Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy made $19.53 billion in profit last quarter. Yet MSCI, one of the world’s biggest providers of stock indexes, has decided Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin company no longer belongs in some of its major investment benchmarks.

MSCI’s November review lists “STRATEGY A”—the company’s MSTR shares—for deletion from the MSCI USA Index after trading closes November 30. That also removes the stock from broader indexes that include U.S. companies, such as the MSCI World and MSCI All Country World indexes.

That sounds technical, but the distinction matters: MSCI is not removing Strategy from the Nasdaq stock exchange, shutting down its business, or making it sell Bitcoin. It is taking MSTR out of stock lists that investment funds use to decide which companies to own.

Consider an ETF designed to copy the MSCI USA Index. When MSTR disappears from the list, the fund generally has to sell its shares, regardless of whether the fund manager likes Saylor’s strategy.

This is why it’s bad news for Strategy. It means less indirect exposition to investments.

MSCI adopted new rules in October for so-called non-operating companies. The idea is to keep investment vehicles—businesses that mainly hold financial assets—out of indexes meant to track operating companies. Its screening process considers a company’s operating assets and other financial measures.

MSCI’s deletion list does not spell out exactly which tests Strategy failed. The company, however, argues that raising capital, managing its Bitcoin treasury and issuing financial products amount to a genuine operating business.

In an August letter to MSCI, Strategy called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” It argued that MSCI should be a “mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.”

Strategy also maintains a software business, but Bitcoin now dominates its finances. The disagreement is whether its Bitcoin activity counts as running a company or mainly managing an investment portfolio.

Strategy’s latest quarterly earnings show $19.53 billion in net income. But that does not mean its software customers paid the company anything close to that amount.

Nearly all of its $20.91 billion in reported operating income came from a rise in the accounting value of its Bitcoin. Under rules adopted in 2025, changes in Bitcoin’s market price appear in Strategy’s earnings even when it has not sold the coins. A decline in Bitcoin can produce the opposite result.

Its software division, meanwhile, recorded $125.4 million in quarterly revenue, down 3% from a year earlier. Its $477.2 million in revenue for all of 2025 was slightly below the $486.3 million reported in 2019, before Strategy began buying Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is selling pressure on MSTR, not on Bitcoin itself. Strategy estimated that funds linked to MSCI indexes hold roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of its outstanding common stock. Not all of that necessarily translates into sudden sales, and Strategy says the amount is manageable.

But Strategy has repeatedly raised money by selling shares and other securities, then used those proceeds to buy Bitcoin. If its stock falls, selling the same number of new shares brings in less cash.

So the company would have to issue more shares to raise the same amount—or buy fewer Bitcoin.

That is why a stock-index decision could eventually matter to the crypto market. The exclusion does not force a Bitcoin sale, and it does not guarantee fewer purchases. It could, however, weaken a key source of funding for one of Bitcoin’s biggest corporate buyers.

#5014. Urologists Have Some Hot Takes on Whether Men Should Sit or Stand to Pee

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AROUND THE WORLD—and on Reddit—there’s an eternal debate raging about whether men should sit or stand to pee. In the US, the answer seems like a no-brainer: standing. One YouGov poll found that only 10 percent of American men regularly sit down to pee, while 31 percent said they never do this. (There’s even that viral video years ago of a pastor arguing “a man is someone who pisses against the wall.”)

But that same YouGov poll found that where you wee varies. In Germany, 40 percent of guys actually sit down every time to urinate. About 22 percent of Swedish men, for example, sit down every time, but 28 percent sit down most of the time. Entire threads online are devoted to this question, including a hybrid tactic as a compromise in which a guy pees sitting down at home but stands up at a urinal in public.

Looking beyond preference, is there a right answer to take a leak? One study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics tried to give a definitive answer. Depending on your camp, the answer might validate what you know—or piss you off.

Researchers had no issue finding 52 guys to sign up for this peeing experiment. These dudes had no prior health issues and were between the ages of 18 and 39. The guys were randomly divided into two groups that sat to urinate. Then they would stand to pee. The other group did the same but in reverse order. Between each change in position was a "washout period" of 24 hours where guys did their business as usual.

Researchers tracked how much urine came out and how quickly. So who reigned supreme on the porcelain throne? Well, neither.

Sitting or standing to urinate didn’t change how much pee they got out in each session. There was a slight difference in how fast they got to max flow, though. Men were able to reach their peak speed slightly sooner when they peed sitting down, but researchers say this finding was “unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Meaning, one guy was pissing really hard while sitting, while everyone else peed at a similar rate and volume no matter what position they did it.

The findings are not surprising to S. Adam Ramin, MD, urologist and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists. “If you're a normal, young, healthy male, it will make no difference whether you sit or stand to urinate,” he says. “You will have a good stream either way.”

THE FINDINGS WOULD likely be different for older men, especially those with an enlarged prostate. “Sometimes in older men with an obstructing prostate, sitting to urinate may help them to empty their bladders more effectively as they are able to generate more abdominal force to squeeze the urine out,” says Boback Berookhim, MD, urologist at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital.

HEALTHWISE, NOT REALLY. But if you have a certain preference for one over the other, then there’s no harm in sticking with one position. There's some convenience with standing to pee: You pull it out, do your business, and move on. Peeing this way is “likely to save time,” says Dr. Berookhim.

Sitters, on the other hand, might prefer the position because it’s slightly more hygienic. Dr. Ramin says guys are more likely to splash, sprinkle on the toilet seat, or even miss entirely when they’re standing versus sitting. Plus, sitters might be more likely to wash their hands after every use. Men are 1.5 times less likely to wash their hands than women after peeing—probably where they could use those saved seconds.

Beyond that necessary bathroom etiquette, there’s really no other reason to switch up your tried-and-true urinary habits. Dr. Berookhim says he certainly wouldn’t tell a young, healthy guy to change the way they are using the bathroom if they are already doing fine.

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#5013. Every Lululemon Shoe Ranked: I Tested Them All, and I Have Thoughts

After putting Lululemon’s full shoe lineup to the test, here’s how each pair ranked.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Lululemon set the bar high for athleisure with its buttery-soft leggings, and continues to deliver on that front. However, since it had always been primarily an athletic wear brand, it wasn’t part of the running shoe or walking shoe conversation. But that changed in 2022 when Lululemon expanded into footwear. Since then, the brand has slowly built a following in that category, too.

I originally tried a pair of Lululemon sneakers a few months ago after reading rave reviews, but quickly stopped wearing them because they felt too snug at my usual size. But I kept seeing positive feedback from other people, making me wonder if I wrote them off too soon. After all, Lululemon is known for careful construction, thoughtful tailoring, and high-quality products.

Like many other shoe brands, each of Lululemon’s sneakers is designed with a specific purpose in mind. The brand’s shoes match Lululemon's overall understated aesthetic. While there are a few bright colors here and there, you also have plenty of neutrals and muted shades to choose from. That alone makes them stand out in a sea of eyeball-searing sneakers.

To see what I was missing beyond looks, I tried each of Lululemon’s athletic shoes—BeyondFeel, Split Shift, Wildfeel, and Chargefeel 3—to see which is the best. And since it’s best to know what you’re getting into before you grab a pair just because it matches your favorite gym outfit, I get into the details about each shoe model below. I was surprised at how wide of a range the brand offers: There’s a Lululemon sneaker for just about anything. Still, one had to come out on top. These are the best Lululemon shoes, ranked, based on months of testing.

The BeyondFeel is the shoe I originally passed on before because it ran snug. So, PSA: Consider sizing up if you prefer a roomy fit or have wide feet. While Lululemon says online that these fit true to size, that wasn't the case for me. Once I went up half a size, I was hooked.

The BeyondFeel is Lululemon's max cushioned shoe, so you can think of it like a Hoka Bondi 9 or On Cloudmonster 3. It's designed for everyday use. Think: running errands, power walking, actual running—it's all comfortable in the BeyondFeel.

I noticed a difference from my daily trainers the second I slipped my feet inside. The best way to describe the feeling is like the first time I put on a pair of Align leggings. I was immediately comfortable, with no chafing, pinching, or any other issues.

This shoe has a nice, roomy toe box, giving your feet plenty of room to swell naturally as you go about your day or rack up the mileage. It also has a stable heel and good grip although, heads up: The shoes may squeak a little when you first wear them inside.

Lululemon designed the BeyondFeel differently for women vs. men, adding an extra 2 millimeters of foam at the forefoot to take some pressure off the knees and hips. I wouldn't wear the BeyondFeel for long runs, though—it doesn't have much energy return, which is that slight bouncy feeling you may get in a shoe. But I was happy to log a few miles in them here and there, along with wearing them for weight training and just running errands. Their stylish look and comfortable feel make them a good choice for nearly everyone.

The Split Shift is Lululemon's neutral everyday running shoe, which is another way of saying it's a good shoe for most runners. The first thing you'll notice is how lightweight the shoe is. At 7.8 ounces, it's not the lightest shoe ever made, but it definitely won't feel like your feet are dragging you down when you're logging higher mileage. This sneaker has an equally breezy upper, giving it an overall airy feel.

I really appreciate the springiness of these shoes. It's not so much that it feels like you're running on mini trampolines, but there's a good energy return here to help propel you forward with each step. That's definitely a noticeable change from the BeyondFeel, which has pretty much no energy return by comparison. There's a gusseted tongue that gently hugs your ankle, along with some extra padding around the ankle that prevents rubbing. The outsole doesn't feel as grippy as the BeyondFeel, but it's a good choice for everyday road running.

My only complaint with the Split Shift is that the toe box runs a little narrow. I'm used to running in shoes with a wide toe box, and the Split Shift's smaller width across the toes means they probably won't be my go-to for everyday miles. Like the BeyondFeel, I'd suggest going up a half size if you like a roomy toe box or have wide feet.

Lululemon's Chargefeel 3 looks different from the brand's other shoes out of the box. It has an hourglass shape, with a narrow middle, more room at the toes, and an exaggerated base at the heel for stability. That shape is intentional, since this shoe is made for cross-training, hybrid, and HIIT workouts. The Chargefeel 3 is on the lighter end of weight for a gym shoe at 8 ounces, and it feels light on your feet. Still, it has everything you want in a shoe you'll be doing cross-training in, like a locked-in feeling in the heel, snug laces, and ability to handle lateral movements.

The grip on this shoe is impressive. I was able to stop cleanly while doing direction-changing indoor sprints at the gym, with no squeaking. The shoe also features a ShiftFoam midsole for a little energy return. Its not nearly as bouncy as the Split Shift, though—but you don't want that in a shoe you'll be doing hybrid workouts in anyway.

The Chargefeel 3 has a 6mm heel-to-toe drop, which may be high for those looking for a neutral strength training shoe, so it might not be ideal for lifting. It’s laser-cut mesh helps tamp down on foot sweat, along with Nulu fabric heel lining to mimic the feel of your favorite leggings.

And if you're looking for a running shoe, scroll up. This is really a gym shoe that you can do a little running in in a pinch—not something you want to do any significant mileage in. And while the Chargefeel 3 made me feel locked-in and secure during gym workouts, it's not so comfortable that I'd wear this shoe outside of exercise. If you're looking for a dedicated hybrid shoe, though, it's worth a look.

Some athletic shoe brands will slap deep lugs on a sneaker and call it a trail shoe without addressing other needs. But it's clear that Lululemon's Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There's a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you're going down. Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. That wasn't a huge deal on shorter runs, but it started to annoy me on longer runs. Like many others on this list, I'd consider going up a half size.

My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that's pretty common in a trail shoe. (It got better with time and more wear.) It's also worth noting that the Wildfeel isn't the most breathable shoe you'll find, and my socks were a little sweatier than usual because of it. None of these are dealbreakers. But it also meant the Wildfeel was my least favorite shoe in Lululemon's lineup.

To choose the best Lululemon shoes, I put each through regular testing over several months. I used each shoe on a near-daily basis for weeks, making sure to test it for the way it was designed. So, I wore the Wildfeel on trails and the Split Shift on daily training runs. During each testing session, I took notes on the shoe's fit, traction, stability, and overall comfort. From there, I ranked each shoe based on its testing results, along with how well it matched up to their intended use.

The best Lululemon shoe for running depends on the type of running you plan to do. If you’re in search of a neutral everyday trainer, the Split Shift is a good choice. It’s lightweight and slightly bouncy, giving you plenty of support and cushioning over daily miles. The BeyondFeel is another solid option. It’s highly cushioned for maximum comfort, making it a better choice for shorter runs.

The best Lululemon shoe for HIIT workouts is the Chargefeel 3. This sneaker has a unique hourglass shape to create a locked-in feel you’ll appreciate during HIIT workouts, along with a wide base for stability. The shoe’s grip is impressive, allowing you to stop quickly and change directions during indoor workouts.

Lululemon used to offer the Strongfeel shoe for strength training, but it’s been discontinued. Now, the Chargefeel 3 is the best option for many strength training workouts due to its wide base and stable platform. But as noted above, the shoe has a higher heel-to-toe drop of 6mm, so it’s not ideal for moves like deadlifts. So if lifting is your priority, you might want to consider a more neutral shoe for optimal biomechanics.

Lululemon often says online that its shoes fit true to size, but that wasn't my experience. I don't have wide feet, but I do appreciate a roomy toe box to accommodate the natural foot swelling that happens on workouts and runs. Most Lululemon shoes tend to run narrow across the toe box. If you have wide feet or just prefer more room to spread your toes, consider going up a size.

Meta’s employee trial advances its prediction market push as Kalshi and Polymarket battle state gambling lawsuits.

Meta has started internal testing of a prediction market app with its employees that would let users compete on guessing the outcome of events without putting real money on the line, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday.

The app, now going by the name Takes, lets users bet "cred" points, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. Similar to other mainstream prediction markets that use money, correct predictions on Takes earn cred while wrong ones lose points.

The testing phase follows June reports that CEO Mark Zuckerberg directed employees to build a standalone prediction market app that would use points, though Meta had not ruled out eventually allowing real-money betting. At the time, the app was going by the name Arena.

The Journal's report does not say whether real-money contracts remain a possibility. Meta declined to comment or give a timetable for a public release.

It comes as real-money platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket are facing lawsuits from states that accuse them of offering illegal gambling. The platforms maintain that their event contracts are legal and fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government.

Speaking at the Cantor Convergence conference on Friday, Commodity and Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig criticized states for pursuing criminal charges against prediction market executives, adding that the disputes should be raised to the Supreme Court.

"Somebody says it's gambling, somebody says it’s a derivative," Selig said. "That's not something that should be at the risk of going to jail."

#5011. North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korean hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months using a social-engineering scheme built on secretly recorded footage and AI deepfakes, the U.S. Justice Department said Thursday, as it announced the seizure of the infrastructure behind the operation.

The scheme, which the FBI calls “FaceStealer,” turns video conference calls into a trap. According to the DOJ, hackers lure targets into meetings using accounts stolen from previous victims, then play prerecorded webcam footage of trusted contacts to simulate their presence and win the target’s confidence.

The group also generates deepfake videos of well-known figures in the crypto and related industries, using AI to make the ruse more convincing.

Once a target is at ease, the attackers manufacture a fake technical glitch, such as claiming the person can’t be heard, and offer a link to “fix” it, which instead installs malware.

From there, the hackers can drain crypto wallets or exploit the victim’s access to other systems, sometimes waiting months or more than a year before striking. The FBI said it seized over 900 webcam recordings of FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant.

The DOJ tied the operation to North Korean groups known variously as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff and APT38, among others, and warned the hackers have increasingly targeted open-source software developers in an apparent bid to enable supply-chain attacks.

The announcement came paired with an update on the record-breaking Binance hack. The department said it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen from the exchange on Oct. 29, part of over $2.7 billion frozen so far.

The FBI attributed that theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and the regime has been laundering the proceeds at speed, spinning up a new wallet roughly every 25 seconds. North Korea has denied involvement, calling the FBI’s finding a political provocation.

The actions underscore how central crypto theft has become to Pyongyang’s finances. The U.S. recently sanctioned 11 people over a North Korean IT-worker scheme that moved millions in crypto, and researchers have cataloged the many ways the regime’s hackers break into crypto firms.

Officials said efforts to trace and recover the stolen Binance funds are ongoing.

But, over the past year, this one has outperformed all the rest and become my go-to top for all kinds of workouts. Whether I’m heading to barre, getting ready to lift, or lacing up my sneakers for a run, I know this top will do exactly what I need it to.

I’ve worn the Super Sleek Bra Tank in quite a few contexts: to the gym, to different types of workout classes, to physical therapy, and even while running. It’s also cute enough and offers enough coverage to wear around town running errands, but I tend to reserve it for working out.

While I wouldn’t usually trust something with a built-in bra on its own for higher-impact workouts, the Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank can handle it. Trust me, I’ve worn it for a 10K race. To be fair, I don’t have the highest demand when it comes to sports bras (if you know what I mean), but thanks to the support features, I think quite a few chest sizes could wear this as a standalone bra-tank combo.

This top is made with Alo’s signature Airlift material, which is made from a sleek blend of durable polyester and stretchy elastane—aka it offers high compression with just enough stretch. Compared to that super soft material you might get in a comfy yoga pant, this top feels more like what you’d get in a classic athletic compression short. It’s a bit thicker, slicker—and it is opaque, so you can feel comfortable wearing it around in public.

The compressive material is also why the top is so supportive. It fits snugly to the body, keeping everything locked in place, while also managing to not feel restrictive or too tight. It also has removable pads (which I lost in the washing machine months ago!), but I’ve found that I don’t need them because the material is so snug. To note: Because it has a tighter fit, the brand recommends that you size up if you have a bigger cup size. (My usual size worked just fine for me.)

Part of the reason I wore this for my 10K race was simply that it looks better on me than just about every other workout tank I own. I think that’s mostly thanks to the compression of the garment, which gives it a smoothing effect and helps make me look snatched.

It has a low scoop neck cut with a racerback silhouette. The longline fit hits a bit lower on your torso than a regular bra would, giving it the look of a cropped tank with the fit of a supportive bra. I love that I can throw this on without worrying about an extra layer and feel a little more covered up than when I head to the gym in a regular sports bra. That said, sometimes I wish it were a bit longer, but most of my workout bottoms are high-waisted, so it ends up feeling long enough.

If you are looking for a bra-tank combo, the Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank is just about the top of the line. The garment’s high-compression, stretchy fit is perfect for a wide range of activities, while still staying comfortable and looking cute. My next move? Buying this top in every color.

#5005. Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Josh Hawley wants Congress to hit the brakes on new data centers, just as lawmakers are moving forward with legislation intended to make building the infrastructure behind America's AI boom easier.

The Missouri senator called for a nationwide moratorium Wednesday, listing it among five priorities for Senate Republicans during the six weeks before Democrats take control of the chamber.

“Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks?” Hawley wrote on X. His answer included a moratorium on data centers, alongside defunding Planned Parenthood, suspending the gas tax and other Republican priorities.

A spokesperson told Politico that Hawley wants a federal pause until Congress passes a “bill of rights giving taxpayers guarantees of no rate increases.” Hawley has not presented detailed legislation specifying which projects would stop or how long the freeze would last.

Data centers are the warehouses packed with powerful computers that train and operate services such as ChatGPT. Building more AI systems means installing more servers, which requires additional electricity, cooling equipment and often upgrades to local power grids.

Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks? Here you go:DEFUND Planned ParenthoodMORATORIUM on data centersSUSPEND the gas tax FUND rural hospitals SAVE AMERICA ACT

— Josh Hawley (@HawleyMO) November 11, 2026

The scale helps explain the concern. U.S. data centers consumed an estimated 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, according to figures cited by Pew, and that could climb to 426 by 2030. In other words, their annual electricity demand could more than double in six years.

On Monday, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a proposal backed by lawmakers from both parties and President Donald Trump's administration.

The bill would speed federal reviews for energy projects and transmission lines, helping bring new power supplies online. It would also require data center operators to pay the additional grid costs their projects create, rather than shifting those expenses onto ordinary electricity customers.

In practical terms, Congress is considering how to keep construction moving without making households subsidize it. Hawley is asking lawmakers to stop new construction until consumer protections are in place.

His position is not entirely new. In February, Hawley introduced the GRID Act with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, seeking to make new data centers obtain electricity from their own sources rather than relying on existing grid supplies.

He now joins independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in publicly supporting a national pause. Their moratorium proposal goes further, calling for rules addressing AI's effects on workers and public safety as well as the environment.

The politics have shifted quickly. In the November 3 elections, voters backed restrictions on data center development across the country, including local bans and measures requiring public approval before construction.

A Pew Research Center analysis published Wednesday found 60% of Americans uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, including 54% of Republicans and 68% of Democrats. Another survey found 58% disliked political leaders who support building data centers near them.

Opponents worry about rising bills, water consumption and noise. Cities have already imposed restrictions, while OpenAI recently promised to cover electricity and grid costs at future campuses it owns and operates.

Industry supporters see a bigger economic risk. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned last month that a construction moratorium could trigger a recession because so much investment now depends on AI infrastructure.

A federal construction freeze could delay the additional computing capacity that AI companies expect to bring online, along with the power infrastructure built to support it. Existing data centers would not necessarily shut down, but the scope of Hawley's proposed moratorium remains undefined.

Hawley's call does not freeze a single project, and he has not said whether he would support the Sanders bill. For now, the Senate is debating legislation to speed infrastructure approvals, not legislation to ban new data centers.

#5000. Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC), chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, has asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, widening a congressional inquiry that has moved from Huang's private life to U.S. controls on chip exports to China. "The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote in a tweet announcing the requests on Thursday evening.

In a letter dated November 12, Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily at a public hearing on December 3 over public reports that "raise significant national security concerns." The committee has jurisdiction over export controls, "including their application to NVIDIA's exports of advanced semiconductors," he wrote. If Huang does not appear, the committee "is prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas."

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

Scott asked Lutnick to testify on December 10, noting Commerce's "central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations." A Lutnick spokesperson told NBC News that he had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily," while the White House said President Donald Trump "maintains complete confidence" in Lutnick.

Separately on Thursday, the Republican chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees, Reps. Brian Mast (R-FL), John Moolenaar (R-MI) and Rick Crawford (R-AR), wrote to Huang, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department's under secretary for industry and security.

Huang was asked to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1 and Teter on December 2, with each given until 8 p.m. on Friday to agree or face a subpoena. Kessler, whose bureau administers export controls, was invited to a hearing on December 3.

"As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and MegaSpeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three chairs said in a statement. They called on Congress to add four chip security bills to the annual defense authorization bill.

It is their second request. A letter dated November 4 had asked Huang to brief the committees on November 18. Mast told reporters on Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers, NBC News reported.

At the center of the inquiries is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials suspected the company of helping Chinese firms get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, The New York Times reported in October. Its sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the Times.

Megaspeed told the Times it had hired outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia has said it complies with U.S. export laws, according to NBC News.

The Times reported that U.S. officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, was a Chinese intelligence asset. China has rejected that as a smear, and Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion on whether she was a spy, according to BBC News.

Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife and resigned on Thursday. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Moolenaar told reporters that Huang had "been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls," Roll Call reported. On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), the Banking Committee's ranking member, and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) asked Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve records on Nvidia chip exports to China.

China's foreign ministry warned on Friday that tighter U.S. export controls on semiconductors would threaten the stability of global supply chains, Al Jazeera reported.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% at $166.19 on Thursday and were up 2.7% at $170.63 in premarket trading early on Friday, according to Yahoo! Finance. The company has lost almost $500 billion in market value since the close on Friday, November 6. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under interim CEO Colette Kress.

#4999. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, exits board; shares plunge

Colette Kress will remain Nvidia’s chief financial officer while serving as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent successor.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president and CEO and stepped down from the company’s board on Thursday, effective immediately. The board named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.

Kress will retain her role as CFO while Nvidia’s board considers internal and external candidates for the permanent CEO role. The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones its first chair and said it expects Nvidia’s operations to proceed without interruption.

Nvidia shares fell more than 13% shortly after the US market opened on Thursday, trading at $151.00 as of 2:31 p.m. UTC, according to Yahoo Finance. Bitcoin (BTC) fell alongside Nvidia shares, dropping as much as 3.5% to a multimonth low.

The shares later pared losses to trade at $165 at 4:24 p.m. UTC, down 5% on the day. The stock was down more than 26% over the previous month.

Kress has served as Nvidia’s CFO since September 2013 and previously held finance positions at Cisco and Microsoft.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter financial results on Nov. 17.

Huang’s departure comes just four days after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation amid reports that the company’s co-founder had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The board said it had no reason to believe US national security or Nvidia’s confidential information had been compromised, but would examine all available information.

In a separate message to employees that day, Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair and apologized to his family and colleagues. He also pledged to cooperate with the investigation.

The Associated Press identified the woman involved in the affair as Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had concluded she was passing information to Beijing. China has denied targeting Huang.

On Tuesday, Nvidia’s independent directors retained former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the inquiry.

On Wednesday, reports said Nvidia’s board was preparing to remove Huang as CEO.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as its CEO for more than 33 years, overseeing its transformation from a graphics-chip maker into a leading supplier of AI processors. His departure marks the first CEO transition in the company’s history.

Nvidia’s market capitalization surged from approximately $57.5 billion at the end of 2016 to a peak of $5.5 trillion on Sept. 1, 2026, a nearly 96-fold increase, according to data from Stock Analysis.

Amid Nvidia’s sell-off, Huang’s estimated net worth fell to $140.6 billion as of 3:42 p.m. UTC Thursday from $162.2 billion on Nov. 9.

House lawmakers still want to question Jensen Huang about his contacts with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against foreign espionage, Rep. John Moolenaar said Thursday.

“We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us,” Moolenaar told reporters, according to Politico.

Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, and fellow committee chairs Rick Crawford and Brian Mast first requested a closed-door briefing in a Nov. 4 letter. They cited concerns about Beijing’s access to sensitive US technology and information and asked Huang to confirm by Nov. 11 whether he could attend on Nov. 18 or to propose another date.

Moolenaar said the lawmakers were prepared to subpoena Huang if they could not agree on a date. He also wants to determine whether Chinese intelligence gained access to sensitive information and examine Huang’s lobbying to ease US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China.

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he was considering forming a subcommittee to investigate the matter when the new Congress convenes in January.

#4998. The 7 Best Garmin Watches, Tested by Our Fitness and Tech Experts

Garmin has a watch for every type of athlete and budget.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Brands like Whoop, OURA, and Apple offer some of the best fitness trackers available, but Garmin watches remain the go-to for serious athletes and outdoor enthusiasts. Men’s Health editors have trusted these wearables to go the distance during ultramarathons, multi-day hikes, and backcountry ski trips thanks to their weeks-long battery life and pinpoint GPS accuracy. But they’re equally useful for everyday life and weekend warriors—we love wearing the Garmin Approach S70 for golf rounds because it comes preloaded with more than 43,000 courses from around the world.

The current Garmin lineup is more robust than ever, from entry-level running watches to premium expedition-ready models that cost upwards of $1,000. Several models come with full-color topographic maps, military-grade durability, and hardcore activity-specific metrics. For instance, runners get detailed stride analysis, cyclists receive power metrics, and swimmers enjoy stroke detection. They also offer specialized outdoor capabilities, including barometric altimeters for precise elevation tracking, compass sensors for navigation without GPS, and pulse oximeters that help monitor your acclimation at high altitudes.

The Garmin Vivoactive 6 offers health monitoring features like sleep coaching, recovery time recommendations, and training readiness scores. Meanwhile, adventure-focused models like the Garmin Instinct 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro incorporate multi-band GPS for accuracy in dense forests, plus emergency features like fall detection and SOS alerts. Whether you’re tracking your first 5K or planning a summit attempt on a remote peak, there’s a Garmin designed specifically for your needs. We’ve logged thousands of miles testing these watches to help you find the perfect match.

Over the years, our editors have done it all: ultramarathons, multi-day backpacking trips, open water swims, and mountain expeditions. Through our adventures, Garmin watches have consistently proven their worth on our wrists. To find the best Garmin watches, we evaluated several models across multiple activities, testing their GPS accuracy, battery performance, and usability. We also considered factors like comfort during prolonged wear and durability when subjected to the elements. This testing allowed us to see how each watch performs out in the real world beyond the spec sheet.

The Fenix 8 stands as Garmin’s ultimate performance watch, offering detailed training insights and reliability for marathoners, ultra-runners, and multi-sport competitors. The watch doesn’t doesn’t track your runs—it analyzes every aspect of your performance with features like training readiness, recovery time, and PacePro technology, allowing you to plan your race-day strategy with GPS-based pace guidance. These features can help you optimize your performance.

Battery life remains exceptional even during GPS-intensive activities. While the standard 51mm AMOLED version delivers approximately 29 days, the solar-equipped model extends this to 48 days with adequate sun exposure. The watch offers multiple power management profiles that let you customize battery usage based on what you have planned that day. This ensures you have the data you need from start to finish without worrying about mid-race charging.

Beyond its training capabilities, the Fenix 8 serves as a reliable navigation tool during unfamiliar routes and trail races. The full-color topographic maps, turn-by-turn directions, and ClimbPro feature help you strategize your effort on challenging courses. You also get comprehensive recovery features, with detailed sleep tracking, HRV status, and body battery energy monitoring that help prevent overtraining.

While the Fenix 8’s price places it among the most expensive sport watches available (especially for the new Fenix 8 Pro), serious athletes who spend hundreds of hours training for major events will find the watch’s performance insights and bulletproof reliability well worth the investment. "This watch has everything that Garmin has to offer into a low-profile casing," says MH Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. "Rugged enough to perform in tough terrain, but sleek enough to fit in everywhere else."

The Vivoactive 6 is one of Garmin’s more lifestyle-oriented models, offering a balance between everyday smartwatch functionality and robust fitness tracking. With its sleek design and comprehensive tracking features, it’s a solid alternative to the Apple Watch SE for those who want longer battery life (up to 11 days) and more comprehensive fitness metrics.

Through running and strength training sessions, the Vivoactive 6 offers detailed metrics about VO2 max, aerobic and anaerobic output, and exercise load. These insights provide a clearer picture of fitness progress than basic calorie and distance tracking. The responsiveness during workouts particularly stood out during our side-by-side comparison with the Apple Watch SE. When increasing running pace, the Vivoactive 6 updated immediately, while the Apple Watch lagged noticeably behind. During strength training, we appreciated the live heart rate zone updates, making it easier to gauge workout intensity in real time.

The most significant advantage over the Apple Watch is battery life. While our SE required daily charging, the Vivoactive 6 kept going for days between charges—a game-changer for active users. The comfortable fit works well even on smaller wrists, and at $299, it offers more fitness functionality than similarly priced competitors while maintaining everyday usability. It supports contactless payments and can even store music from your favorite Spotify playlists. If you want comprehensive fitness insights without the premium price, the Vivoactive 6 hits the sweet spot.

The Forerunner 970 is Garmin’s new flagship running watch, built for athletes who want every data point without sacrificing everyday usability. It pairs a brighter 1.4-inch AMOLED display with a built-in speaker and microphone, plus a tougher sapphire lens and lightweight titanium bezel, so it feels premium yet rugged enough for hard training.

During intervals and long runs, the interface is intuitive—pace, heart rate, and distance are all visible at a glance, and after each session the watch prompts you to rate how the run felt. The 970 also offers deeper performance tools, including running economy, running tolerance (when paired with Garmin’s HRM 600 chest strap), hill score, endurance score, and more detailed load analysis to show how hard you’re pushing week to week.

Battery life remains a major selling point. Garmin claims up to 15 days in smartwatch mode and 26 hours in GPS mode with multi-band SATIQ, so you can stack long runs, races, and daily training without worrying about charging. Built-in full-color maps, turn-by-turn directions, dynamic round-trip routing, ClimbPro, and Up Ahead make the watch just as useful on unfamiliar trails as it is for neighborhood miles.

Recovery and health tracking also see significant upgrades over older Forerunners. Training Readiness delivers a simple morning score based on recent sleep and workload, so you know whether to push or back off. Upgraded sleep tracking, nap detection, and newer tools like ECG readings also provide a clearer picture of how your body handles stress, illness, and heavy training weeks.

If you’re looking for something that’s durable, look no further than the Instinct 3. The watch offers military-grade construction that can withstand some real punishment, with a rugged design that proved its worth throughout testing. We accidentally banged it against doorways and scraped it against kettlebells during workouts, yet it emerged without a scratch. The distinctly masculine aesthetic features a substantial case housing an impressive array of sensors while maintaining water resistance to 100 meters.

Battery performance is one of the Instinct 3’s most impressive features. While Garmin claims 18 days between charges, our testing revealed closer to 21 days of regular use without heavy reliance on battery-intensive features. It makes it one of the longest-lasting watches in Garmin’s lineup, while providing a significant advantage over other mainstream smartwatches. When you do need a recharge, a quick 10-minute session can add several hours of use—perfect for those who forgot to charge before heading out the door.

For trail runs and hikers, the watch includes a digital compass that shows your precise directional heading, multi-band GPS with SatIQ technology, and a built-in flashlight with multiple intensity levels including a red light option. The Instinct 3 also features ABC sensors that provide real-time environmental data. Of course, the watch also offers powerful health and fitness features, including HRV status, stress tracking, and the ability to track your blood oxygen levels.

Read more: Our Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED Review

Don’t let the lower price tag fool you: The Forerunner 165 packs serious running tech into a $249 package, making it the ideal option for runners who are just getting started on their journey or those looking to dip their toes into fitness trackers. This relative newcomer to Garmin’s lineup boasts an AMOLED display, a lightweight design, and advanced training metrics runners will appreciate.

Despite being positioned as an entry-level running watch, the Forerunner 165 outclasses similarly priced competitors with its premium build quality and thoughtful design. It’s incredibly comfortable, especially compared to Garmin’s bulkier models, while still maintaining the brand’s impressive durability. The AMOLED screen offers excellent readability even in bright sunlight, and text looks crisp. We particularly appreciated the intuitive physical button navigation combined with touchscreen functionality.

For runners who want their first serious training companion, the Forerunner 165 hits the sweet spot by delivering Garmin’s core running analytics without overwhelming users. While it lacks some of the advanced recovery tools found in the Forerunner 965 like Training Readiness, it covers all the essentials with accurate GPS tracking and guided workouts.

The Venu 4 is Garmin’s latest lifestyle smartwatch, and it feels like a smarter, more polished upgrade from the Venu 3. Available in 41mm and 45mm sizes, it pairs a bright AMOLED display with a metal case and a low-profile design for a clean, casual look that looks great both at the office and at the gym.

In testing, the Venu line has always stood out for being easy to live with, and the latest model doubles down on that. Battery life stretches up to roughly 12 days in smartwatch mode depending on how often you’re working out and using the always-on display, which means you don’t have to baby it with nightly charges—topping it up during a shower a few times a week is usually enough. The built-in LED flashlight is also a welcome addition for running at dusk or dawn, helping you stay visible to drivers. You also get a speaker and mic for taking calls and using your phone’s voice assistant from your wrist.

What makes the Venu 4 more than a standard smartwatch is that it treats your health as more than just steps and heart rate. Health status and lifestyle logging show how daily choices—like drinking caffeine later in the day—actually affect your sleep, stress, and heart rate variability, so the data feels more useful than just a bunch of charts. The Venu 4 also has the new Garmin Coach feature, with over 80 preloaded GPS and indoor sports apps that cover everything from walking and HIIT to yoga and strength training.

Its app and ecosystem integration still isn’t as far-reaching as an Apple Watch, especially on iPhone, but if you care more about deeper health tracking and better workouts, the Venu 4 is a great alternative that offers multi-day battery life and more recovery-focused insights.

The Approach S70 is the ultimate golf companion, delivering comprehensive course coverage—with over 43,000 preloaded courses worldwide—in a sleek, lightweight design. Available in two sizes (42mm and 47mm), this premium golf watch displays detailed course maps showing precise distance to greens, hazards, and doglegs, while the Virtual Caddie feature provides club recommendations based on your playing history and current conditions.

What truly sets the S70 apart is its attention to golf-specific details. The watch provides front, center, and back distance readings to every green, along with precise yardages to hazards. This is extremely helpful as sometimes you can’t even fully see a hole and have no idea that a water hazard is lying within distance of your next shot, so that overview of the hole is crucial info to have. The "plays like" feature accounts for elevation changes and wind when calculating distances, something that can be difficult to gauge on your own.

Beyond the thousands of preloaded courses, the S70 also displays green contour data to improve your putting strategy (Garmin Golf membership required). During our testing, the functions and how to navigate them took a little getting used to, but once we got that down, it was pretty easy after every shot just to twist our wrist to get our next distance. The AMOLED display has also been crisp and never difficult to see out in the sun.

At $699, the S70 is a significant investment, but for golfers who regularly play and want and easy way to gauge the shots to hit, the combination of golf-specific features and modern smartwatch functionality makes it a great companion on the course.

Read More: Our Review of the Garmin Approach S70

Depending on the Garmin you choose, you can expect battery life to last anywhere from a few days to a few weeks. The Fenix 8 AMOLED’s battery can stretch for up to 16 days, while the Fenix 8 with solar will go up to 21 days (28 days with solar). Of course, real-world battery performance can vary based on how you actually use your watch. Running a marathon with continuous GPS tracking? You’ll drain the battery much faster than if you’re just checking notifications and tracking daily steps.

Garmin has a reputation for offering several advanced training and recovery metrics, which can help you understand how ready your body is for exercise and optimize your training schedule. The Forerunner 970 offers Training Readiness, which synthesizes your sleep score, recovery time, acute training load, sleep history, and more to show "when you are most likely to benefit from a hard workout and when to consider dialing down to let your body catch up," Garmin says.Even if you don’t train every day, you can still benefit from Garmin’s more basic tracking features, like daily step count, calories, and sleep. Some models can even track your stress, monitoring your body’s physiological responses throughout the day. During a hectic workday or high-pressure meeting, knowing when you’re stressed can prompt you to take action—i.e., perform breathing exercises—which can make a difference in your overall well-being.Additionally, Garmin’s various models analyze detailed performance metrics to determine if your training is productive, offer built-in coaching features to prepare you for races, and suggest workouts tailored to your fitness level and goals. What makes Garmin’s approach so good is its flexibility—serious athletes can drive into the data, while casual users can stick with simpler metrics and guided programs.

GPS and Garmin go hand in hand, so it’s no surprise that the brand’s watches offer robust tracking and navigation. These features can be essential for runners, hikers, and outdoor athletes. Most Garmin watches provide detailed maps, turn-by-turn directions, and breadcrumb trails that help you retrace your steps. Some high-end models, like the aforementioned Fenix 8, offers offline maps with enhanced satellite imagery, SATIQ technology, ABC sensors, and more. These features can be invaluable for precise tracking even in steep valleys, offer reliable compass headings, and deliver accurate elevation readings.

Garmin watches traditionally prioritize function over fashion, packing them with a lot of tech and large batteries. As a result, they generally skew larger compared to many competitors. Some models come in multiple sizes—the Venu 4 is available with screen sizes of 41mm and 45mm, similar to the Apple Watch Series 11, which comes in 42mm and 46mm. However, the Venu 3 is still noticeably larger; it boasts a width of 45mm and a thickness of 12mm (compared to the Series 10’s 36mm and 9.7mm). That said, some of Garmin’s watches, like the Forerunner 970, only come in one size. If you have smaller wrists like I do, you have two options: Buy your preferred model and accept that it might look oversized on your wrist, or opt for one of Garmin’s more lifestyle-oriented models like the Vivoactive 6, which is 10.9mm thick. Garmin does offer "S" variants of several models specifically designed for small wrists—the Venu 3S, for example, is thinner and lighter than the normal Venu 3. However, these S models typically sacrifice battery life for their smaller footprint, so you’ll have to consider if that’s a compromise you’re willing to make.

There are a lot of Garmin watches to choose from—the brand lists five major lineups on its website. The Forerunner 165 is one of Garmin's most affordable models at $249, providing you essential training metrics, built-in GPS, and up to 11 days of battery life. The more full-featured Venu 4 jumps up in price to $549, offering more detailed health insights, better battery life, and a larger, more vibrant display. Garmin’s premium adventure watches command the highest prices, with the Fenix 8 starting at $899 and climbing to $1,099 for solar-equipped models with sapphire crystal displays. When deciding which Garmin is right for you, consider what features you truly need versus what’s nice to have. If you’re a casual runner, you might be best served by something in the Forerunner lineup. But if you regularly go hiking in the backcountry, you might find the premium price of a Fenix justified by its comprehensive navigation tools and extended battery life.

#4994. Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Leading cryptocurrency Bitcoin has dropped 5.6% on the day, and is currently trading at just over $69,300, per Decrypt data. It comes after the latest consumer price index, or CPI, results came in "hotter than expected," experts said, with the drop was triggered by a "concentrated liquidation."

Bitcoin's plunge took it to a 24-hour low of $67,922, its lowest level since mid-August, when it boosted from $63,000.

"Bitcoin’s drop below $69,000 was directly triggered by a concentrated liquidation of leveraged long positions," Tim Sun, senior analyst at Hashkey, told Decrypt. "Though the deeper issue lies in steadily weakening market demand."

Sun highlighted U.S. Bitcoin spot ETFs recording six consecutive days of net outflows, according to CoinGlass. He also pointed to stablecoin supply shrinking and MSCI removing digital asset treasury firm Strategy from its funds.

"ETFs, stablecoin liquidity, and corporate treasuries have served as the primary capital pillars supporting this Bitcoin rally," Sun said. "With all three coming under simultaneous pressure, the market is losing the marginal buying power that previously propelled prices higher."

Meanwhile, other major cryptocurrencies have also taken a hit. Ethereum has dropped 4.6% on the day to $1,953, BNB has slipped 4.7% to $639.46, and Solana is down 3.1% to $80.47, according to Decrypt data. The global crypto market cap has dropped 4.6% over the past 24 hours to $2.39 trillion.

It follows U.S. CPI rising 0.4% in October, which is "hotter than expected, even if the headline monthly rate eased to 0.4% from September’s 0.6%," according to CoinShares head of research James Butterfill. "More troubling was the composition," he added. "Food rose 0.5%, services remained firm, and core CPI increased 0.3%, with services excluding rent, a gauge of domestic price pressure the Fed watches closely, rising 0.5%. The inflation problem is therefore no longer easily dismissed as an oil story."

The consumer price index, or CPI, is a way of measuring inflation that tracks the average price changes of everyday goods and services over time. Central banks tend to use CPI to inform whether they'll cut or hike interest rates, meaning higher-than-expected CPI signals a potential Federal Reserve hike.

Polymarket predictors put a 97% chance on the Fed raising interest rates this year, up from 75% at the start of the week. The CME FedWatch tool, meanwhile, sees an 88% chance of a 25 basis point hike, with 12% anticipating a 50 basis point rise.

On top of the CPI, Bitcoin's downward move comes following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company, after reports of multiple affairs including with a suspected Chinese spy and a senior company executive spread.

Huang's departure has sparked "severe volatility across tech stocks, further dampening market risk appetite," Sun told Decrypt. "This has prompted broader portfolio de-risking, amplifying the downward pressure on Bitcoin," he added.

For a crypto rebound to happen, Sun said that Bitcoin needs "long-term allocation capital" to flow back into crypto after ETFs, stablecoins, and digital asset treasury companies have taken a hit in recent weeks.
