#4974. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

North Korean hackers launch memecoins to launder funds stolen in the Binance hack, while xStocks plans to add hundreds of Hong Kong-listed equities in the coming weeks.

North Korean hackers created memecoins to launder cryptocurrency stolen in the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to a report from blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.Between Nov. 5 and 7, the hackers created at least six tokens on NEAR and used liquidity pools on decentralized exchanges to move $430,000 of stolen funds between wallets, Elliptic said. However, the tokens attracted almost no outside trading and were abandoned shortly after launch.

Elliptic said the same laundering technique was also used following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025, when North Korean-linked actors moved at least $24 million through a newly created token on the TRON blockchain.

Hong Kong’s wealthy investors are embracing crypto. (Chi Hung Wong)

Kraken parent Payward’s xStocks platform has added tokenized versions of more than 200 stocks listed in the United Kingdom and European Union.

Payward said the latest expansion brings xStocks’ offering to more than 1,500 tokenized assets. The company reported more than $45 billion in cumulative transaction volume and over 550,000 unique holders.

Payward said it plans to add hundreds of Hong Kong-listed equities in the coming weeks.

#4972. The 7 Best Portable Basketball Hoops and Systems for Any Yard or Driveway

If you want to ball out at home, these are the hoops for you.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

If you live by the "ball is life" moniker and you need to be able to play at home, a portable basketball hoop is a must. Portable basketball hoops don't require you to perform manual labor like digging a huge hole in the ground and pouring concrete, nor do they cost over a thousand bucks. Another plus to going portable? You can store your hoop come winter, thus lengthening its lifespan. It’s also a solid option for those who don't have the time, money, or space to install an in-ground option but still wanna toss their basketball shoes on and shoot around a bit quickly.

"I feel like the portable hoop is what transformed me into who I am," NBA shooting coach Chris Matthews (a.k.a. Lethal Shooter) says. "My cousin Justin and I would play on the portable hoop at his house when we couldn't make it to the playground. He had a garage light, and we would shoot all night."

You can make memories like that in whatever space you have for the court. But don't get caught buying a hoop that’s a waste of money. Not all hoops are the same, so we’re here to cut through the noise. Here are some of the best options we came up with.

Spalding makes a handful of portable goals, but the Momentous EZ is our favorite due to its value-driven price and ease of assembly. Spalding notes it takes about 30 minutes to put together. We found it took just over that time when following the instructions, which makes it the easiest goal to assemble in our book.

As Matthews notes, "The more portable a basketball hoop is, the better, so that everyone can move it. That's one reason I like the models from Spalding."

As for the materials in the hoop, the Momentous EZ comes with an acrylic backboard in either 50- or 54-inch sizing. You can also choose between a clear view back, an H-frame, or a steel H-frame (for added support and durability). We chose the steel H-frame to help prevent backboard damage. The theory behind the H-frame is that it should help absorb stress when someone dunks or hangs on the rim.

There's a hand crank for adjusting the height of the goal (simple to use if you have kids or if you want to do a driveway dunk contest). The base is wide and supportive and will hold up to 26 gallons of water or sand. If you're looking for a premium goal that won't set you back a thousand dollars, there's nothing better than this pick. Start here in your search. You won't regret it.

More: The 6 Best Basketballs for Indoor Games and Street Hoops

If you are looking for a portable goal that won't break the bank, this top-selling $250 model is worth a look. It's made to adjust to a wide range of height, from 4.8 feet to 10 feet. This means it appeals to everyone from small kids to adults. One cool idea you can do with this goal is you can lower it to its 4-foot setting and position it up against an in-ground pool—something other goals in this guide don't have a low enough range to make it suitable for pool hoops.

The biggest qualm about this one is the polycarbonate backboard. It won't last as long as acrylic, and you should expect a few good years out of it with a slight decline in bounce as it braves the changing of the seasons. One way to help preserve this goal, though, is to store it inside whenever possible to avoid weathering.

Lifetime is another brand that churns out long-lasting portable goals. This one is similar to the Spalding Momentous EZ with a wide acrylic backboard. The base is also just as sturdy as the Spalding EZ, and it has an ability to hold up to 35 gallons of water or sand. The downside of this goal to the Spalding EZ is it's not as fast of a setup, so you do need to lock in for at least two hours to get it up.

The upside? That would be the 4 extra inches of backboard, the reinforced rim, and the hand crank adjustment. The rim is thicker and outfitted with steel springs, which makes it a lot more capable for handling dunks. The hand crank makes adjusting the goal from 7.5 feet to 10 feet smoother and easier than the turning hand crank on the Spalding EZ goal.

The Spalding has the easier setup and price, but Lifetime has a few premium features that will make competitive play more fun.

The FORZA Adjustable Basketball Hoop and Post System earns its place as a “Best Adjustable Hoop for Growing Players” thanks to its flexible height settings and portable design. Built for both kids learning their first shots and adults looking for competitive backyard games, the hoop adjusts from youth-friendly heights to regulation size, making it a long-term investment rather than something your kids quickly outgrow. Its wheeled base also makes it easy to move across driveways or patios, adding convenience for families who want flexibility.

Designed for indoor or outdoor use, the hoop features a sturdy base and adjustable frame that can accommodate players of different ages and skill levels. This versatile hoop can come out when you're hosting weekend family games or serious practice sessions, but be stored when not in use. There are also optional upgrades available.

This model from IE Sports will help save you some cash while still providing decent play. Its made with a 44-inch polycarbonate backboard, which is great when it comes to saving money. The base and frame are similar in design to the Awii Sports option, so there's no worries on durability here.

Like mentioned prior, we don't really like the hand crank for adjusting the height; this goal has one. You've probably noticed the unique mini trampoline this goal comes with so you can pass the ball to yourself. We think it's an awesome feature, as it maximizes solo practice by allowing you to work on passing and catch-and-shoot drills. Overall, this goal is reliable, well-priced, and comes with a fun feature.

Remember how fun mini hoops are? This goal takes mini hoops to a whole other level with an adjustable height pole (up to 7 feet) and a sturdy base. Sure you could buy a cheap sub-$100 full size goal for your kids to play with, but for a similar price you get a much better build and a whole lot of fun.

Position it up to your pool for water mini hoops. Bring it down to your basement or put it in the garage for winter mini hoops. You get the point.

The Huupe Mini Hoop is the perfect nostalgia pick for any guy, regardless of age. It is quite literally the most portable hoop on our list, with the ability to be tossed on any door. This smart hoop has a wide variety of virtual games you can enjoy. The hoop comes with some heft, namely from the technology, which allows you to test your shot against others online, or even watch your favorite streaming apps.

"I think that mini hoops like the Huupe are another great option for families that don't have room in their garage or a driveway," Matthews says. "It's a great way to have kids to get energy out during the day, even when the weather is not ideal. They are easy to install, too."

In any case, it's easily installed using the classic over-the-door mount. You can also wall mount, but you need to buy those parts separately. There are special sensors throughout the device, which follow your shot as well as your distance from the hoop. This means it can reliably track your shot so you can get better after every game. One of our testers even said, "I enjoyed using this hoop to shoot around with my toddler daughter, and when I just wanted to play around a little bit by myself, it was awesome to get to watch the NBA playoffs on the screen as I shot."

Chris Matthews (aka Lethal Shooter) is a world-renowned shooting coach to NBA stars like Jaylen Brown, Dwight Howard, and Anthony Davis, and WNBA star Candice Parker.

Having spent countless hours as kids growing up playing pickup games in driveways, we know a thing or two about a solid portable basketball hoop. Men's Health Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, has played lots of basketball and helped us dial in on the proper picks for this guide. Considering all those firsthand experiences led us to find the best of the best. Factors like backboard material, adjustability, and special design notes were considered in our selection process. We also took into account price, as some basketball goals provide a better overall value than others.

In addition, we also consulted world-renowned basketball shooting coach Chris Matthews (a.k.a. Lethal Shooter) on what makes for a good portable hoop. Our guide below represents our top picks, all approved by Matthews, of portable basketball hoops that will actually last for years to come. Keep scrolling to learn more.

Not every hoop is going to have the same adjustability in terms of how low or high you can raise it. This is crucial if you have little ones and want the whole family to partake in the fun. It’s also a great way to put on a dunk contest if you still have the bunnies, too. There are also different mechanisms built for adjusting, such as a hand crank, a telescoping pole, pneumatic assist, or a gas spring.

The types of materials used directly impact the long-term durability of your hoop. The two types of backboard materials to know about for portable basketball goals are acrylic and polycarbonate (there's also glass, but glass is used for professional backboards and is extremely rare on portable ones). Polycarbonate is going to be cheaper, but the tradeoff is that exposure to weather and UV light will make the backboard brittle and rigid over time. Acrylic is typically more expensive, but the benefit is that it's better suited for exposure to weather and UV light (acrylic is not affected by UV light like polycarbonate), plus you get a more responsive bounce.

Basketball rims are not all created equal. If you’ve ever been to a park court, you know what we mean—one slightly off shot and your ball rockets across the street. There are a few common materials you’ll see: steel and double-rimmed steel, powder-coated rims, and occasionally composite or plastic. You’ll also see that there are breakaway rims, standard, and flex.

To keep a portable basketball hoop in place, you'll need to fill its base with something. Most portable goals hold about 35 gallons, and you can either go with water or sand. We prefer sand because it dissipates well. Sand is also denser than water, so filling the base with sand is wiser for a more secure hold. However, choosing water makes it easier to empty the base and refill, making it easier to maneuver, especially if you need to move elsewhere in your driveway (or take it to your neighbor's for a friendly pickup game).

If you're curious about how much weight you need to keep your goal in place, a safe number is around 300 to 450 pounds. It sounds like a lot, but if you want to be safe and protect your goal, then more weight is always worth adding. And keep in mind that they all include wheels attached to the base to move them more easily. If you want to eliminate the labor of filling the base full, you can fill it to a point and then stack sandbags on top of the back of the goal to keep it in place. It won't be the most pleasing to look at, but it will allow you to move the goal around more easily.

Paying more gets you a better playing experience, especially when it comes to a wide acrylic backboard. A wider backboard makes it easier to shoot bank shots and perform layups, and the acrylic material will be much more responsive and last longer. A more expensive goal might also come with better wheels for moving the goal. Keep in mind a portable basketball hoop won't be as deluxe as an in-ground one, but you can get pretty dang close.

A regulation backboard is typically 48 inches tall by 72 inches wide. Most portable hoops have a 48-inch height, but there's a variance on width. While 72 inches is fun to play on due to the full ability to shoot bank shots and layups, a driveway goal doesn't need to be that wide.

Look to a 50-inch or 54-inch width. Anything under 50 is fine; however, you will lose space to shoot bank shots and layups. The benefit to buying a goal with a smaller backboard, though, is that you save money (they're almost always cheaper).

The easiest way to store a portable basketball goal is to lower the rim to its lowest setting, tarp it, then roll it into a garage or shed. Some basketball hoops can be disassembled (or at least partially disassembled), but that process can be pretty annoying. Make sure to drain any water from the base to avoid it freezing and expanding the plastic of the base.

Some of the high-end Spalding portable goals can partially disassemble for storage (not the Spalding EZ we recommend, though). You can take out bolts at the middle of the goal, and the backboard will fold down, thus helping store it in a garage or shed with a low ceiling.

#4970. Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Britain's new crypto rules will still be in transition when global anti-money laundering assessors arrive next year, and the country will be judged on whether it can enforce against crypto laundering, a taskforce convened by the Royal United Services Institute has warned.

The report, published on Friday, sets out the issues the London-based defense and security think tank's taskforce expects to dominate the UK's 2027 evaluation by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). The Paris-based body sets global standards against money laundering and terrorist financing, and its peer reviews, known as mutual evaluations, grade countries on whether their rules work in practice.

The UK's report is due to be agreed at FATF's February 2028 plenary. The taskforce, made up of experts from the private sector, law enforcement and civil society, met in September; its discussions are not attributed to individual members.

This will be the first UK evaluation in which FATF considers crypto, and the taskforce was clear that crypto is a "material risk" for the UK. The City of London Police assesses that 66% of investment fraud in the UK involves crypto, according to the report, while the UK's 2025 National Risk Assessment rated crypto money laundering high risk, up from medium in 2020.

The UK brought crypto firms under its money laundering rules in 2020, and legislation passed in February created a statutory crypto regime. The Financial Conduct Authority set out which crypto activities it will regulate in April and finalized its rulebook in June, but the mandatory regime does not take effect until October 25, 2027.

The taskforce doubted the UK would be able to show adequate implementation by the time FATF visits in June, and said the UK had moved more conservatively than Hong Kong, the EU and Singapore.

Members were unanimous that assessors would examine this, and pointed to over-the-counter brokers, which the National Crime Agency estimated in the 2025 risk assessment are likely to launder hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

The taskforce cited the Metropolitan Police's £5.5 billion (about $7.3 billion) crypto seizure, linked to a Chinese professional money launderer sentenced in 2025, as an encouraging sign of what the UK criminal justice system can do when it has the capacity. But one member said the success had not been repeated in enough cases, and that the UK had barely scratched the surface of crypto laundering. FATF is expected to test whether results match the risk rather than rest on one headline case, the report said.

It also warned that because the UK's regime, which resembles the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, focuses on identifiable crypto firms, it risks pushing the highest-risk crypto outside the FCA's perimeter. That would leave law enforcement to trace assets the regulator cannot reach, such as Tether's USDT, with the taskforce pointing to a July 2025 Treasury report that flagged the stablecoin as having been "extensively exploited" by Russian-speaking laundering networks. Members doubted law enforcement had been given the capability and resources to keep pace.

The taskforce did praise UK international cooperation, including Operation Destabilise, which targeted Russian-speaking networks converting street cash into crypto. But it flagged resourcing of the UK Financial Intelligence Unit and law enforcement's economic crime capacity as likely vulnerabilities.

FATF has been pressing countries on crypto enforcement more broadly. In July, it said nearly 93% of jurisdictions it surveyed had yet to apply its standards to qualifying DeFiplatforms.

So over the past few months, I made it my mission to track down the best white t-shirts for women. It might seem simple, but the details matter: the perfect tee should have just the right amount of stretch, a flattering drape, and be thick enough to wear on its own.

A white tee that ticks all those boxes is really the ultimate wardrobe essential, says celebrity stylist Julie Matos. It's the layering MVP that looks just as good with jeans as it does under a blazer. The tricky part is finding one that nails the trifecta of fabric, fit, and finish. Too often, white t-shirts are overly sheer, stiff, or cut in a way that doesn’t flatter the body. But after testing dozens, I can confirm: The perfect white t-shirt exists, and it’s worth the hunt.

So, are you ready to finally discover the perfect white tee that you can easily wear all year round? Start with this tried-and-tested guide.

After testing what feels like every white t-shirt on the internet, the Agolde Adine Shrunken Tee easily won my heart. It layers well and looks great on its own—it’s a true staple in my wardrobe that I wear about once a week. It has a relaxed silhouette and shorter (but not quite cropped) length that makes it super easy to style on its own with jeans or under a blazer or leather jacket. Oh, and it isn’t see-through at all.

It’s made from 100 percent organic cotton and has that thick, substantial feel I love in a t-shirt. Its weight gives it a luxe feel, even though the design is simple. That’s why it's thick enough to be worn with a nude bra, but still breathable and soft against the skin. Plus, it holds its shape well after multiple washes—I’ve been wearing and washing this tee at least once a week for the past year—no shrinkage, loose threads, or pilling in sight.

This tee nails that lived-in, vintage look that makes it look like you’ve owned it for years in the best possible way. Matos loves this t-shirt for that “fitted but not too tight” silhouette, and I totally agree. It’s structured enough to avoid looking sloppy, yet still relaxed and casual. The shrunken cut adds the right amount of shape, flattering my frame without too much extra fabric. The length seals the deal: it hits right at the waistband of my mid-rise jeans, so it looks perfectly balanced.

Between the fit, the feel, and that easy, slightly worn-in finish, the Adine Shrunken Tee truly is the white t-shirt gold standard. I’ve been wearing it nonstop—with jeans and a blazer to the office, layered under a sweater, or under a zip-up hoodie and sweats for laid-back errands.

#4967. A Good Pair of Pickleball Shoes Can Help Improve Your Game. Here Are Our Top Picks.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Improve your game with the latest pickleball-ready shoes.

PICKLEBALL IS A fun way to stay fit, which is especially true if you have the proper gear. This ensures you can make the most of all your matches, which starts from the ground up. Buying a pair of pickleball shoes is one of the smartest investments you can make in your game. Unlike your pickleball paddle, your pickleball shoes have a much more direct relationship to your health. Two of the most important factors to consider are traction and stability.

Like tennis shoes, pickleball shoes need to handle quick movements in all types of directions. That means you want strong outsoles with responsive tread patterns and a midsole structure that can handle fast-twitch lateral movements. Lateral stability is super important since it can help prevent common pickleball injuries to ankles or knees, so it’s more important for them to have a wider base and a stiff lower structure to provide this kind of maximum stability. Our guide to the best pickleball shoes will set you up with the right kind of shoe for enhancing performance while hopefully reducing the odds of rolling an ankle or spraining a knee.

DOWNLOAD OUR ULTIMATE PICKLEBALL WORKOUT PLAN PDF

The Rush Pro Ace Pickleball is designed for both indoor and outdoor court surfaces and has a 4D Support Chassis for controlled pivot movements and stability. When we tested it out, The Pickler held tough through all the wear and tear.

The rubber drag pad has helped protect tearing on the end of the toe box, and the cushioned midsole helps keep high foot arches comfortable. The Pickler even has a rebound-like effect when making fast-twitch movements, which makes sense because of how close in construction the shoe is to Pro Ace Tennis Shoe—Wilson's top-selling model for tennis. The rebound of the shoe alone isn't going to make you a better player, but we do believe it helps promote staying on your toes more during play, especially when it comes to getting into a firefight against opponents.

The performance on this shoe is superb, and the style promises a clean look that's suitable for wearing in a country club environment. The comfort of the shoe—namely the supportive arch and cushioned padding around the tongue and ankle—became the final selling point to deem these the best pickleball shoes overall in 2026.

If you’re getting into pickleball for the first time, you don’t want to spend close to $200 just to find out it isn't for you. A great affordable pickleball shoe can help you there—it’s also a great option for those who simply like to budget, too. Enter the second iteration of the Asics Gel-Renma pickleball shoes. A stellar shoe for under $100.

Loaded with similar tech and materials you’ll find in Asics pro-level models, this pair uses a synthetic leather overlay for solid durability as well as its signature Trusstic tech, which helps to enhance stability. To help create a shoe that’s well-balanced for all directional movements, it uses a wrap-up outsole with flex grooves for increased flexibility, and a wider gauge. As Winn notes, "Asics has skyrocketed to the top over the last few years," and this pair is one affordable, high-performance pair.

You might be surprised to find K-Swiss at the top of the pickleball shoe market, but the brand has quietly been creating trusted game-ready models for all types of price points. We've come to find the Express Light as one of the top supportive and strong pickleball shoes money can buy.

Two main features of this shoe stood out when testing: the 180-degree Plantar Support Chassis and the DURAWRAP cover to help combat toe dragging. The support chassis worked great at providing a secure feeling while playing, giving ample support for high arches and preventing feet from twisting and rolling inside the shoe—even when they go hot and sweaty. The DURAWRAP cover is the outsole material used to combat abrasion and toe-dragging. The cover is definitely hard alright, and so it's nice to know you have this strong outer shell over the cushioned mesh that feels oh-so-good on the feet.

The shoes do fit quite snugly, so consider potentially going up a half size on this shoe. The design is unique, and fun with multiple colorways. It's not the fastest shoe, but it provides great durability and support. This is a well-balanced model you can play outside in for long periods of time.

If you’re looking for one lightweight, serious pair of pickleball shoes that can also handle the wear and tear of aggressive game play, the second version of the Viper Courts are definitely the way to go.This go around features a revamped upper that makes them even more durable than the previous gen, while remaining just as breathable and potentially even more comfortable (at least popular opinion says, according to reviewers).

These low tops feature quite the supportive feel with their EVA insoles and responsive foam in the midsoles that are topped off with Goodyear Gold compound soles that can take all the quick cuts and bursts you’ll find yourself doing every game. Plus, they’re versatile enough for the other two big racket sports of tennis and Padel.

New Balance takes the cake when it comes to shoes for those in need of a little extra stability. Both instructors we talked to agree that New Balance always delivers on comfort, support, and above all, stability. Between the precise underfoot cushioning, superior durability, or the FuelCell foam, the elements all come together to form a thoughtful design.

"They're well-made, so they last a long time and are very comfortable," Winn says. Armstrong also adds, "Looking around and asking a few of our senior players, [the New Balances] seem to be a fan favorite." At the end of the day, comfort and stability are the leading factors in selecting a shoe for seniors, both of which this shoe excels in, according to Armstrong.

Babolat doesn't just make stellar tennis racquets; the brand's tennis shoes are in a league of its own. With a soft upper and ventilated mesh, the SFX 4 delivers comfort and breathability in each wear. Babolat doubles down on the comfort with an OrthoLite insole that molds to the shape of your foot. A premium cushioning system absorbs shock in landings, which is super important for comfort and keeping your knees feeling good after a match. The shape and composition of the materials in the sole are segmented into nine key pressure points to deliver maximum responsiveness.

Armstrong also recommends these shoes for beginners. "In my experience, beginners need to look for something that may not require a huge investment, but also provides all the benefits needed to play tennis comfortably and safely," he says. "Generally, the shoes that are in a new player's price range and then feel the best, are the best shoes for them."

Pickleball is a social event and if you want a pair that can go from the courts to drinks afterwards, these Pickle Pro is our choice for sure. With their modern design and streamlined look, you could probably toss on a pair of slacks while wearing these and get away with it. I have worn them out in public running errands multiple times already and have even gotten several compliments on them, they’re that sharp.

Aesthetics aside, these shoes can still hold their own on the courts thanks to their solid design. For starters, these are darn comfortable with their OrthoLite foam midsoles that make them quite plush for a pair of pickleball shoes. Comfy as they are, they are quite tough too, which stems from the Duralast high-density soles that grips well on all court surfaces, but, it does mean they take a bit to break in from my experience. While I wouldn’t necessarily choose them for ultra competitive games, for a stylish and casual game, these are an absolute winner.

The Barricade is a go-to for all training sessions and matches for players who prioritize comfort. When shopping for shoes, Armstrong says, "Players have different criteria as to what makes a shoe great. Personally, I want something that is durable, supportive but not too bulky, and comfortable." Armstrong, who teaches/plays almost every day of the week, needs something that feels good on his notoriously aching Achilles tendon. Adidas makes this pair that does all of this, and are even a favorite of Armstrong's father (who tore his Achilles a few years ago) because of their unrivaled comfort.

Wonder why? It might have something to do with the shoe's foam Geofit Sensepods to securely lock in the heel, a cushioned Bounce midsole, and asymmetrical laces to help guard against the effects of foot drag. There's also a sustainability component, with 50 percent of the yarn in the upper being recycled.

If your the type of player who loves to chase down every shot, you’re going to need a shoe that can keep up. That means you’re going to want a pair that flexes and moves with your natural foot strike, allowing you to stay light on the balls of your feet. One of the best in the game right now that allows just those types of movement patterns are the CourtStrike Pro 2.0s from Selkirk.

Thanks to their 3D printing, you get a secure shoe with excellent lateral stability and a super responsive EVA midsole that helps to drastically improve you're reaction time. This allows you to stay explosive and react at will.

This 2.0 model features better, more durable rubber, extra material protection along the bottom of the laces for increased longevity, and multiple layered cushioning for a springier step. If you’re on a budget, you may want to opt for another pair on our list, but if you want one of the most versatile pairs around, just get these.

Pickleball shoes need to provide support, so buying the lightest shoe possible is not the smartest move. When buying a lightweight shoe (say, under 10 ounces) there's likely to be some sacrifice in support or stability. The trick? Stick to pickleball-specific shoes first. You can also consider tennis shoes and cross-trainers due to their similar support-first construction. Avoid featherlight running shoes that are built for a different type of movement.

Mesh is the most common and best material to look for in the upper of a pickleball shoe. However, like weight, you don't necessarily need the most breathable mesh possible. Some pickleball shoes sacrifice breathability to boost abrasion resistance, and to help keep your foot secure (like limiting your foot rolling and turning inside the shoe).

When it comes to the outsole, look for a shoe that has a strong rubber pattern that will help grip surfaces and reduce the odds of slipping when turning your feet. Some pickleball shoes pay greater attention to tread pattern, which can help provide a feeling of better grip on a court. Outsole will largely come down to personal preference, as most are constructed about the same.

When looking at the midsole, aim for a shoe that has supportive cushioning (like EVA foam) and keeps a relatively low profile. Prioritizing a midsole with too much cushioning could lead you to a shoe that sits high (like a Hoka running shoe), thus leading to a less responsive design, which could potentially lead to a greater chance of rolling an ankle when making fast turns on the court.

I have been fortunate enough to rock quite a few pairs of pickleball shoes over the past few years. Having played on multiple surfaces, I’ve learned a few things about what to look for when selecting a pair. I also partnered with our other writers and editors at Men's Health to help select the best pickleball shoes we’ve tested in the past few years, available. We’ve compiled a guide to the best all-day play, taking great note of each shoe's stability, durability, weight, and price point. Special consideration was taken into account for pickleball shoes that had excellent traction and stability since those two qualities are the most important in a pickleball shoe.

There is a lot of crossover from effective tennis shoes to pickleball shoes. So we also spoke to experts like Life Time Galleria Tennis Leader Gary Armstrong (who has been playing tennis for 36 years and has been an instructor for 17 years) and Life Time Charlotte Tennis Leader Eric Winn (who has been a tennis coach for 24 years and still plays in the 5.0 USTA leagues) to get their takes on the best tennis shoes for men. With minimal differences, some of their picks made it to this guide.

If you're someone who's going to play pickleball once or twice for recreation, then you could get away with a low-profile running shoe. But if you're expecting to play any more than that, we strongly recommend buying a proper pair of pickleball shoes.

The reason we don't recommend wearing just any type of running shoe is that running shoes are made for forward motion, so there's often less emphasis on reinforcing the shoe for side-to-side movements. Running shoes also have less structure and stability than what you want in a pickleball shoe, as the running styles these days are made to be as lightweight and breathable as possible (with high cushioned stacks), which means less focus on overall support.

So, to be clear, you should steer from wearing running shoes for pickleball if you expect to play the game on a regular basis. A proper pickleball shoe is a smart investment that will help give you traction and stability while greatly decreasing the chance of rolling an ankle or spraining a knee.

#4965. Bitcoin Hits 12-Week Low as Fed Rate Fears Undo Most of Summer Rally

Bitcoin Hits 12-Week Low as Fed Rate Fears Undo Most of Summer Rally

Bitcoin fell to roughly $68,500 on Friday, hitting its lowest price in 12 weeks as renewed U.S. inflation worries and investor withdrawals pushed the cryptocurrency further into the red.

BTC was down about 4.5% over 24 hours and 9.5% for the week, according to Friday market data. Ethereum traded near $1,925, while Solana slipped below $80 as selling spread across major cryptocurrencies.

The latest slide has erased most of Bitcoin's late-summer recovery. But not all of it: BTC remains approximately 16% above its late-June low near $59,000, even after retreating roughly 21% from its autumn peak around $86,000.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee warned Friday that inflation had spread beyond energy and tariffs, with rising services and medical costs and demand from AI data centers adding to price pressures.

“Are we on a path back to 2%? My feeling right now is we are not and we've got to deal with that,” Goolsbee said according to Reuters.

Goolsbee did not explicitly endorse a December rate hike. But other Fed officials have been more direct.

On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he supported raising interest rates by at least 25 basis points, or 0.25 percentage points, at the December 8-9 meeting.

He also established a threshold for considering something more aggressive.

“If the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed,” Waller said in his official remarks.

The report subsequently showed core CPI rising exactly 0.3%, exceeding the 0.2% forecast and meeting Waller's condition for considering a 50-basis-point increase.

Markets have responded accordingly. Futures-based rate probabilities as of November 13 showed a 91.9% probability of a quarter-point increase and an 8.1% probability of a half-point increase.

Those figures reflect trader expectations, not a decision by the Fed. The central bank's current target range is 3.75% to 4.00%.

Friday's producer-price report added to the concerns. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, less than forecast, but increased 6.5% year over year, the largest annual jump since 2022.

For Bitcoin, higher rates make traditional interest-bearing investments relatively more attractive, reducing the appeal of speculative assets.

Meanwhile, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have registered six consecutive sessions of net outflows, totaling approximately $1.49 billion between November 5 and November 12.

Thursday's $47.7 million withdrawal extended the five-day outflow streak, bringing another source of pressure to an already struggling market.

That does not mean institutional investors have abandoned Bitcoin. The funds still hold approximately $55.5 billion in cumulative net inflows, but it does show the state of nervousness that investors are feeling.

Weakening ETF demand, combined with forced liquidations of leveraged traders, can accelerate a decline when buyers are scarce.

Bitcoin's daily chart now shows a clear sequence of lower highs and lower lows, confirming a bearish short-term trajectory.

Its relative strength index, or RSI, has dropped to 25.4. Readings below 30 are generally considered oversold, suggesting the selling may be stretched.The average directional index, or ADX, stands at 25.3, indicating an established trend. Combined with declining prices, that suggests bearish momentum remains meaningful.

There is still one longer-term positive signal: the 50-day exponential moving average remains above the 200-day EMA, preserving a bullish moving-average configuration. But Bitcoin's price has fallen below the shorter-term average, indicating that recent momentum has turned against buyers.

Immediate support sits around $67,650, Friday's intraday low. Losing that level could expose a deeper support area near $64,000.

On the upside, Bitcoin needs to recover $70,815 and $72,775 before challenging the stronger resistance zone between $74,355 and $75,937.

The combination of extreme oversold readings and strong downward momentum leaves room for a temporary bounce, but not enough evidence to declare a bottom.

For now, traders face two major macroeconomic checkpoints: the Fed's November 18 meeting minutes and the November 25 PCE inflation report, both of which could influence expectations ahead of December's interest-rate decision.

#4962. Maple Finance’s strategy rift sends co-founder, COO to the exits

Maple Finance co-founder Joe Flanagan and COO Ryan O’Shea are leaving over disagreements about the firm’s direction as SYRUP falls despite revenue growth.

Two senior executives are leaving onchain asset manager Maple Finance over disagreements about the firm’s direction as its SYRUP token slid more than 7% Thursday.

Maple co-founder and executive chairman Joe Flanagan said Wednesday he would leave after seven years at the firm, describing a growing divide with fellow co-founder and CEO Sidney Powell.

“Over time, our views on strategy, leadership, and life have moved further apart,” Flanagan wrote. “I believe Maple is best served by one co-founder leading it forward from here.”

Chief operating officer Ryan O’Shea also said in a Thursday post on X that he would leave after nearly five years at Maple. “I’ll be stepping down as COO. I’ve come to a different view on the direction Maple should take, and I’ve decided it’s time to step aside,” he wrote.

SYRUP traded at $0.12 at 10:36 p.m. UTC Thursday, down 7.5% over 24 hours and 12% over the past week, according to CoinGecko. The token had a market capitalization of about $145 million.

Maple and Powell did not respond to Cointelegraph’s requests for comment by publication.

In a statement published Wednesday, Maple confirmed that Flanagan was stepping down as chairman and leaving the company. “This is an agreed and orderly transition,” the company said, adding that his responsibilities would move to Powell and Maple’s existing leadership team.

The company did not announce a replacement chairman or specify how the departing executives’ duties would be carried out.

Flanagan said his differences with Powell reached a point where they were no longer constructive. “I am choosing to leave rather than continue supporting a direction I cannot stand behind,” he said. Flanagan added that he would help with the transition through the end of 2026.

O’Shea is stepping down effective Nov. 27. “I’ll have no ongoing role after that,” he wrote.

The departures come as Maple looks to expand beyond crypto-backed lending. In October, Powell said the firm planned to reach more customers through fintech partnerships and lend against a wider range of assets, including payments owed on loans made by fintech companies and securities backed by assets such as mortgages.

Related: Kraken, Maple launch onchain warehouse facility for crypto-backed institutional loans

The announcements come as Maple’s lending business continues to grow, while SYRUP is down 62% year to date and total value locked (TVL) has declined.

According to Token Terminal, Maple’s protocol revenue rose 8% year over year in October, while TVL fell around 11% between the end of September and Nov. 11.

Maple’s latest quarterly results also showed growth, with the company reporting $4.4 million in third-quarter revenue, up 5% from a year earlier. Assets under management rose 18% year over year to $4.7 billion.

Maple has also been using some of its revenue to buy back SYRUP tokens. In September, the company repurchased about 1.37 million tokens, twice as many as in August, according to its October update.

#4960. Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

President Donald Trump has nominated four people to fill vacant seats at the two federal agencies writing the rules for crypto, in a bipartisan slate that could reshape the commissions that have increasingly taken the lead on digital-asset policy after Congress stalled.

The White House said Thursday it sent the nominations to the Senate: Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and Kristin Johnson and Steven Levine for the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Each requires Senate confirmation. Notably, the slate pairs a Republican and a Democrat at each agency, with Anonick and Levine the Republicans and Rowland and Johnson the Democrats, marking the first time the administration has put forward Democratic nominees for either commission.

The appointments matter because of how depleted both agencies have become. The CFTC in particular has been running on a skeleton crew, operating with Michael Selig as its lone Senate-confirmed member after a wave of departures, even as it has pursued one of the most aggressive crypto agendas in its history.

Filling those seats would give the commissions the quorum and staying power to turn proposals into durable rules.

Both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which shares jurisdiction over crypto market structure and will vet their nominations. Anonick, a Republican, is legislative counsel to committee Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the panel’s portion of the Clarity Act, the crypto market-structure bill that collapsed in the Senate this fall.

Rowland, a Democrat, is a career CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and an earlier 2024 crypto bill. His enforcement-heavy background and party lean could introduce a dissenting voice to a commission that, under Selig, has leaned firmly pro-industry.

On the SEC side, which the Senate Banking Committee will review, the picks would replace two commissioners central to crypto policy in opposite ways. Levine, a Republican, is slated to fill the seat of Hester Peirce, the agency’s most prominent crypto advocate and the head of its Crypto Task Force.

Levine’s own views on digital assets are not well established publicly, making his future votes a key variable for whether the SEC’s crypto-friendly push holds.

Johnson, a Democrat and former CFTC commissioner, would take the seat of frequent crypto skeptic Caroline Crenshaw; at the CFTC she focused on digital-asset custody and DeFi and pressed for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules.

The timing underscores a shift following the collapse of the Clarity Act, the crypto industry’s marquee market structure bill that would have established more-favorable-than-not rules for most of crypto.

After the legislation failed to advance in the Senate, the SEC and CFTC moved to fill the vacuum with their own authority, leaving the industry to get its “clarity” from regulators rather than legislators. A fully staffed pair of commissions would cement that dynamic.

Those agency efforts have been sweeping: The CFTC has cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, floated bringing crypto exchanges under federal oversight, and moved to define event contracts as “swaps.” The SEC, meanwhile, rolled out an “innovation exemption” for tokenized stocks, proposed rules letting investment advisers custody crypto, and issued guidance suggesting most crypto assets aren’t securities.

The nominations are the first Trump has sent for these seats in roughly a year, a gap that reflected turbulence around crypto appointments. The administration previously pulled its CFTC chair nominee, Brian Quintenz, amid a clash involving the Winklevoss twins.

The confirmation window is now tight: with the Senate heading toward Democratic control in January, Republicans have only a short lame-duck stretch to move the slate before the calculus changes.

#4958. Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low

Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump.

Crypto exchange Gemini has just reported its lowest quarterly retail trading volume in three years, despite an increase in overall crypto trading volume.

Total spot trading volume rose 18% from the second quarter to $4.5 billion, according to Gemini’s Q3 earnings report. Institutional volume climbed 26% to $3.9 billion, while retail volume fell 14% to $600 million, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023.

Gemini said the quarterly increase in spot trading volume was “supported by increased institutional Zcash activity and expanded affiliated market-making,” but did not give a specific reason for the decline in retail trading.

Despite the retail slump, Gemini’s exchange revenue increased 7% from the previous quarter to $13.4 million as institutional revenue more than doubled. Retail traders remained its largest source of exchange revenue, contributing nearly three-quarters of the total.

A number of crypto exchanges also reported softer crypto trading activity in the most recent quarter.

Coinbase reported softer retail and institutional activity, with consumer spot trading volume falling 9% from the previous quarter to $23.4 billion. Coinbase chief financial officer Alesia Haas said “continued growth in prediction markets helped offset softer crypto trading activity.”

At Robinhood, crypto revenue fell 55% year-on-year to $120 million, offset by a sixfold increase in event-contract revenue to $173 million.

Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off

Gemini also got some help from its own prediction exchange, Gemini Predictions, with revenue from that business unit increasing 52% quarter-on-quarter to $796,000, though it wasn’t significant enough to offset declines elsewhere.

Gemini reported stronger prediction-market activity heading into the fourth quarter, with average daily traders in October running about 50% above the third-quarter average.

Nearly a third of new prediction traders were new to Gemini, more than double the proportion in Q3.

The company is also seeking to distribute its event contracts through other platforms. An August nonbinding agreement with Apex Fintech Solutions would make Gemini Titan the exclusive venue for crypto event contracts distributed through Apex’s futures brokerage to its brokerage customers, subject to definitive agreements.

Gemini is set to host a Q3 earnings call on Friday.

#4957. The 6 Best On Shoes for Walking of 2026, Tested By Fitness Editors and Podiatrists

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a Women’s Health style writer, I regularly test the latest releases from all the major sneaker brands. On kicks are some of my favorites, and our editors and A-list celebs love ‘em too (including Zendaya). The Swiss brand has seen impressive growth over the past year, becoming a major competitor among sneaker giants like Nike and Adidas. On’s signature CloudTec cushioning not only makes you feel like you’re “walking on clouds,” but it’s also right on trend and a major style statement for wellness girlies.

We've named these kicks some of the best running shoes for plantar fasciitis, but after vigorous testing, we absolutely love On shoes for walking, too. Podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, says he walks around the city daily in his On sneakers because they make him feel supported and comfortable and accommodate his Dr. Scholl's insoles. "Thanks to the thicker sole and rounded heel, they provide that perfect mix of function, stability, and cushion without sacrificing any category," he says.

On has a large roster of comfortable sneakers, so it can be tricky to know where to start to find the perfect pair. That's why we tapped Schaeffer, podiatrist Daniel Geller, DPM, and Women's Health fitness editors to give us the lowdown on what to look for when shopping for the best On Cloud shoes for walking: in this case, weight, cushion, stability, and heel-to-toe drop.

Keep reading to see our favorites, and be sure to check out our 4-Week Walking Plan for the perfect workout to break in your new kicks.

After testing several pairs of On shoes, the Cloudrunner 3—a cushier, more supportive upgrade from the Cloudrunner 2—takes the top spot for a few key reasons. Executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos has tested more than a dozen On shoes and says the Cloudrunner 3 has become a go-to in her sneaker collection lately. That’s because the shoe has a relatively lightweight feel with tons of stability.

That balance comes from the sole, which is made with On’s Helion Superfoam. This material, made from thermoplastic polyurethane, blends firm and flexible foam components to create a lightweight, responsive, and well-cushioned feel. The mix of stiffer and softer sections absorbs impact from every step and actually helps propel you forward. The Cloudrunner 3 is actually a touch heavier than its predecessor (by only 0.7 ounces), but we chalk it up to the upgraded plush heel collar and wider base that offer a bit more comfort and stability. I’ve noticed this shoe is super durable, holding up to months of wear and tear on city sidewalks. During my walks in this shoe, I appreciate that I don’t feel overly bouncy, but the cushioning is still noticeable and light enough to help me feel grounded.“At nine months pregnant, I need to prioritize stability and comfort over everything else in a sneaker right now, and the On Cloudrunner 3s delivered for me,” Andriakos says. “It feels firm and supportive (and not overly cushioned), which has noticeably reduced my pelvic and low back pain when I’m on my feet all day and walking a lot.” She’s also been wearing it for hybrid strength-and-cardio workouts, and while it’s not a super-flat traditional lifting shoe, the fairly neutral sole and structured shape and feel make it surprisingly versatile. “Plus, the toe box is on the wider side and roomy enough for my swollen feet, so my toes can actually breathe,” Andriakos adds.

After about four months of testing an alarming amount of shoes, the On Cloudtilt Remix is my everyday go-to. That’s because this sneaker takes everything we love about the original Cloudtilt and gives it a fashion-forward upgrade with a techy upper designed with “X-ray layers,” or semi-transparent mesh overlays that look super sleek.

This shoe is basically built for walking, too, thanks to the CloudTec Phase midsole, a walking-focused cushioning system designed so each “cloud” compresses in sequence, delivering a smooth, plush ride. The result is an exceptionally smooth heel-to-toe transition that feels natural and effortless during long days on your feet. It also has a moderate 7 mm heel-to-toe drop, meaning it distributes weight evenly throughout the lower body and helps keep the foot in a neutral walking position, making it a pretty universal pick.

Underfoot, the cushioning lands squarely in the Goldilocks zone. The Helion superfoam provides plenty of impact absorption, but the ride never feels overly soft or marshmallow-like. Instead, it delivers a lightly responsive, cushioned feel that keeps your feet comfortable during long walks, travel days, and hours of sightseeing without sacrificing ground feel or stability. Lightweight, stylish, and genuinely built for all-day movement, the Cloudtilt Remix is the On sneaker I reach for when I want my shoes to work as hard as the rest of my outfit. The sleek, streamlined look is super easy to style with everything from tennis skirts to joggers to track pants. If you ask me, it’s kinda the perfect shoe that combines everything on this list into one sleek kick.

My one note is that I worry about the layered mesh upper being difficult to clean if the shoe gets too dirty. Luckily, I’ve managed to keep it pretty clean, but I avoid wearing this shoe in wet weather or otherwise messy conditions.

Hate tying your shoes? The Cloudnova Form 2 might be your new favorite—thanks to its easy slip-on, slip-off design, which Andriakos swears by. That said, it still has laces if you want to tighten things up for a more secure fit. This is my everyday shoe when I’m heading out the door to run errands or pop out for a walk but don’t feel like wearing anything bulky or something that needs a full lace adjustment (just lazy girl things!). It looks super cute with sweatpants and leggings, and a boxy t-shirt on top.

Comfort-wise, the Cloudnova Form is a win right out of the box. During my testing, I found that there was no break-in period needed (big ups). The moderately-cushioned sole is super balanced, which makes it ideal for long walks and power strolls, and Andriakos especially likes that it doesn’t have the super-prominent “bubble” look that many On shoes are known for. Instead, it has a lower-cut silhouette that feels a bit more grounded and less bouncy.

Another plus: The Form 2 is made with a breathable mesh upper and a soft microfiber tongue, so your feet stay cool and comfortable even on warm or extra-active days. On the downside, it runs small, so it’s a good idea to size it up by half. Also worth noting: it has a high heel-to-toe drop (14 mm), which can put extra stress on the knees and hips. If you deal with pain in those areas, you might want to skip this one.

On only offers wide sizing for certain models, but this shoe has a spacious toe box for a roomy fit. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi has bunions and never experiences pain when wearing it. “Most sneakers that don’t come in wide sizing tend to irritate and rub against my bunions, which makes them throb, but not the Cloudmonster,” she says. “The toe box is surprisingly a perfect fit and lets me walk around for hours pain-free.”

This new version of the shoe delivers a cradling sensation while the foam slightly compresses to conform to your feet. The sensation is pillow-like under the foot while also offering a stable feel. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton notes that it's her all-time fave On walking shoe for its high-stack cushion, meaning it has a very thick foam between your foot and the ground. The 3 gets back to the Cloudmonster’s roots and becomes a good running shoe for intermediate to advanced runners again. That’s thanks to a speedboard that promotes a forward rolling motion, along with the aforementioned maxed cushioning. This has added only a little weight from the last model (6.6 ounces to 8.5), so you don’t have to worry about this shoe holding you back during long walks or runs.

"Whenever I want to feel super comfortable in my shoes but don't want that tight, locked-in feeling like I do when I'm running, the Cloudmonster is my go-to," Appleton says. She wore the shoe while moving into her fourth-floor Brooklyn walk-up, and notes it kept her feet comfortable all day. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy t-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

The heel-to-toe drop is also on the smaller side at six millimeters, which Accardi says distributes impact evenly on the knees, hips, and ankles. “As someone with knee issues, taking the load off my knees is essential, especially post-run,” she says. If you’re a heel striker and don’t struggle with pain in these areas, the Cloudrunner 2 could be a better fit.

If your workouts don’t fit neatly into one category, the On Cloud X 4 is the sneaker you’ll want on standby. Designed specifically for mixed training, it’s comfortable, responsive, and stable, making it equally suited for walking, HIIT training, and gym sessions. Unlike some of On’s chunkier models, the Cloud X 4 has a slightly lower-profile silhouette that looks and feels sleeker on foot, pairing easily with everyday outfits and activewear.

The shoe features On’s signature CloudTec cushioning, which delivers a comfortable, impact-absorbing ride without feeling overly squishy. Andriakos, who logs a high daily step count, says it’s become one of her favorite shoes for long walks because the cushioning feels nice and plush while maintaining a grounded feel. “The mesh upper is super breathable, so my feet don’t feel overheated and sweaty after long walks, and small design details (like the cool X lace pattern from above!) make it feel really polished,” she says.

The supportive lacing system creates a secure, locked-in feel that feels stable during lateral movements and dynamic workouts. “I’ve worn it to HIIT classes, and it feels super supportive, though I’d still opt for a flatter, more structured shoe for traditional lifting,” Andriakos says. The mesh upper is a nice touch, too, keeping things super breathable so your feet don’t get overheated or sweaty on long walks.

The On Cloud 6 Coast is a refreshed take on the brand’s classic On Cloud—but this ultra-lightweight version takes it even further. It keeps all the upgrades of the latest model, including the original slip-on, no-lace design and On’s signature CloudTec cushioning system. The big win here? It weighs in at just 6.5 ounces. That means your ultra-cushioned shoe is now perfect for traveling, long days on your feet, or hot, humid commutes. It’s built with an updated mesh that’s super breathable and ventilated—you can even wear this shoe barefoot!It also features a wider opening for a more inclusive, easy-on fit. I really appreciated this feature as a wide-footed girly. It also has a moderate heel-to-toe drop of 8 mm, making it a great universal walking shoe. Bottom line: this shoe is made to handle just about anything, which makes it a must-have in your rotation.

This shoe has a medium cushion level for that sweet spot that’s comfortable and light on your feet without being overly plush. The CloudTec midsole does a great job absorbing impact, making it a solid choice for everything from sightseeing and airport sprints to casual daily walks. The lightweight build almost disappears on your foot, which is exactly what you want when you’re packing light or spending hours exploring.

The tradeoff for all that packability and featherlight comfort is support. The flexible upper and minimalist construction can feel a bit flimsy compared to more structured walking shoes, especially if you need extra arch support or stability.

On sneakers are extremely comfortable, but Schaeffer says that's because most of its shoes have a bit of weight to them. If a shoe is too lightweight (under four ounces), it sacrifices function and stability, he says. But, don't get it twisted—these don't feel like bricks on your feet either. Most On shoes are between four and 10 ounces, which means they're the perfect medium weight that doesn’t slack on support.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Support and stability are the number one qualities you should look for in a walking shoe, says Geller. He notes that when arches are supported, you create an "excellent" platform to launch from, meaning the feet are in the ideal position for takeoff and landing. This can help avoid foot injuries down the line.

Geller also says that many good walking shoes, including motion control shoes, will have medial posting—a firm wedge in the arch that holds up the heel—and firm cushioning for more support. "Firmer cushioning will resist the inward roll of the foot [overpronation], controlling the knees and hips better," he says.

If stability is a priority for you, also consider shoes with a broader sole to minimize excess movement. The increased material along the sides and front of your foot creates a wider platform, which is naturally resistant to feet rolling or wobbling, says Geller. In other words, it's a great feature for walkers who overpronate.

"Whenever you’re looking for a good walking shoe, you want to find a great mix of comfort and stability," says Schaeffer. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but the level of cushioning will vary depending on your specific foot needs.

Wearing running shoes for walking isn’t inherently bad, but it’s not always the best idea either. Shoes designed specifically for running tend to have significantly more cushioning to absorb the higher impact that comes with each stride. “This isn't necessary for walking and reduces your feel of the ground, which is problematic for those with any balance issues or previous falls," Milica McDowell, a doctor of physical therapy, previously told Women’s Health.

Running shoes often have a very tight fit for higher performance, a narrow toe box, or are highly supported in the arch, which are features a lifestyle walker does not need, says McDowell. That’s why, in most cases, walkers are recommended to opt for a shoe designed specifically for walking (or one labeled for walking and running).

To curate a list of the best On walking shoes, I tested On kicks for two years, alongside fitness contributor Talene Appleton, NASM-CPT, fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, style contributor Lily Wohlner, and executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos.

We wore them during long and short walks for at least several hours at a time. We evaluated each shoe based on:

We found that the new and older winners all provide top-notch comfort, cushioning, support, and stability through all our long walks.

#4955. Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact

Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will convene a public forum Monday to examine whether artificial intelligence will bring down inflation, drive prices higher, or replace American workers.

The November 16 conference in San Francisco will bring together technology executives, economists, and employers to examine how AI is reshaping the economy.

The findings could influence how the Fed approaches interest rates, a major factor in Bitcoin's price movements as investors weigh whether to put money into risky assets or safer alternatives.

Warsh has argued that AI could help companies produce more goods and services at lower costs, easing inflation without requiring the Fed to keep borrowing expensive.

But some of his colleagues see a different problem: The AI boom is already making things more expensive, while the promised productivity benefits remain largely theoretical.

Building data centers requires enormous quantities of electricity, computer chips, construction materials, and skilled workers. When technology companies compete for those limited resources, prices rise.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned in September that AI investment was adding inflationary pressure and delaying the central bank's return to its 2% inflation target.

If AI eventually allows businesses to produce more without raising costs, inflation could cool, giving policymakers room to lower interest rates.

Lower rates generally make risky assets like Bitcoin or tech stocks more attractive because government bonds and savings accounts offer smaller returns, encouraging investors to seek higher gains elsewhere.

But if AI spending keeps inflation elevated, the Fed could maintain high interest rates or raise them further. That would make borrowing more expensive, strengthen the appeal of interest-bearing assets, and potentially drain money from speculative investments, including cryptocurrencies.

Bitcoin is already feeling that pressure. The cryptocurrency dropped below $69,000 Friday as stronger-than-expected inflation figures fueled concerns about another Fed rate hike.

AI also has a more direct connection to the Bitcoin industry than most may think of.

Both AI data centers and Bitcoin mining operations need access to large amounts of electricity. As AI companies compete for power and infrastructure, miners face pressure to secure affordable energy or consider more profitable alternatives.

Some are already abandoning Bitcoin mining altogether. Hyperscale Data shut down mining operations at its Michigan facility in September to accommodate an AI customer under a deal potentially worth more than $1.2 billion. The same has happened with other big names like Coreweave and other former Ethereum miners from its proof-of-work era.

Meanwhile, AI's potential impact on employment adds another complication.

Fed Governor Michael Barr warned Thursday of possible “serious short-term disruptions” as businesses increasingly replace human tasks with AI systems.

Widespread job losses could weaken consumer spending, slow economic growth, and eventually increase pressure on the Fed to cut rates. But a deteriorating economy could also push investors away from Bitcoin as they look to reduce risk.

Warsh himself acknowledged in August that AI represents “a new variable” for monetary policy.

The question now is whether AI's economic benefits will arrive quickly enough to outweigh the costs of building it.

Monday's conference will not determine the Fed's next interest-rate decision, scheduled for December 9. But it could offer clues about how policymakers view a technology boom that is increasingly influencing both Wall Street and the crypto market.

#4953. Trump nominates Hester Peirce successor among SEC, CFTC picks

The White House also named a former CFTC commissioner and two CLARITY Act veterans as nominees to fill vacancies at the SEC and CFTC.

US President Donald Trump has nominated Steven Levine to replace former Securities and Exchange Commission Commissioner Hester Peirce, one of the agency’s most prominent crypto advocates, as part of four nominations to fill vacancies at the SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The White House’s latest announcement on Thursday named two nominees each for the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, agencies whose decisions help shape US cryptocurrency regulation, among other functions. All four nominations require Senate confirmation.

The nominations would replenish several commissioner roles. The SEC currently has only two of its five commissioner seats filled, while CFTC Chairman Michael Selig is the sole member of his agency’s five-seat commission.

The nominations come weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the Senate in January, giving a narrow window for Republicans to confirm Trump’s picks.

Related: House Finance panel chair says regulator actions on crypto ‘fall short’ of CLARITY bill

Levine, a Republican, was nominated for an SEC term ending June 5, 2030, replacing Peirce, who left the agency in October. Peirce was a leading advocate for clearer crypto rules at the SEC, helping shape its approach to digital assets as the former head of its Crypto Task Force, while Levine’s views on crypto regulation are less publicly established.

Trump also nominated Democrat Kristin Johnson, a former CFTC commissioner, for the SEC seat held by Caroline Crenshaw, whose term has also expired. Johnson’s proposed term ends June 5, 2029. Johnson has advocated for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules for crypto firms in her time at the CFTC.

For the CFTC, Trump nominated Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland, both of whom worked on the Clarity Act. CFTC Chairman Mike Selig called them “two strong bipartisan picks” for CFTC commissioners and said he looked forward to working with them upon their confirmation.

The nominees would typically appear before the Senate Banking Committee for the SEC positions and the Senate Agriculture Committee for the CFTC roles. Following committee consideration, their nominations would go to the full Senate, where confirmation requires a majority vote.

#4950. Bitcoin slides below $70K amid thin liquidity, ETF outflows

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 as crypto sentiment hit its lowest level in more than four months, with analysts warning of institutional outflows, thinning liquidity and elevated leverage.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday, extending its recent decline as investor sentiment deteriorated amid institutional outflows, tightening liquidity and broader macroeconomic pressures.

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading at $68,607.23 at the time of writing, down 9.2% in the last week, according to CoinGecko.

The drop coincided with a sharp decline in market sentiment. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index fell to 20 on Friday, its lowest reading in more than four months, putting it in “extreme fear.” The index last reached that level on July 8.

Bitcoin’s seven-day price chart. Source: CoinGecko

Vikram Subburaj, CEO of crypto exchange Giottus, attributed Bitcoin’s weakness to institutional outflows, tightening crypto liquidity and expectations of a December Federal Reserve interest rate hike. “Investors should avoid chasing short-term dips or using excessive leverage,” he said.

In a Friday report, 10x Research highlighted Bitcoin’s divergence from US equities. Between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12, Bitcoin declined 5.9% while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, suggesting the cryptocurrency was responding more to rising Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar than to technology stocks.

The research firm said Bitcoin was increasingly trading alongside gold, which fell 5.5% over the same period, as the US 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%.

Meanwhile, institutional trading platform Talos also warned that thin liquidity and elevated leverage could amplify market volatility. Its weekly report showed Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels.

“Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” said Tanay Ved, senior research associate at Talos. “A rebuild in order-book depth and a turn in capital flows would provide a firmer foundation for recovery.”

The selloff follows sustained withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs). BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows across nine consecutive trading sessions through Wednesday, while broader funds shed nearly $1.44 billion over five sessions.

Preliminary Farside Investors data showed another $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, although figures for BlackRock and Fidelity were still pending.
